name: Word Safari
one_liner: Hear a spoken word and tap the one of four pictures that shows what it means.
interaction: Four picture tiles appear; a speaker button plays the target word (audio in production; play-button + text caption in this demo). The child taps one tile; the tile locks with a confirming pop. No printed words are read. Word rarity auto-adjusts up/down by a frequency staircase after each answer.
self_teach: Wordless ghost-hand demo (<10s): the speaker icon pulses, then a floating hand glides to the correct picture and taps it with a happy pop. Then one unscored warm-up uses an easy high-frequency word; any tap is accepted with gentle feedback before scoring begins.

learning_science.why: Pairing a spoken word with candidate pictures lets meaning be verified across verbal and visual codes, removing the reading load that would otherwise confound a young child's vocabulary.
learning_science.concrete_decision: Prompts are audio; every response is a picture, never a printed word.
learning_science.source: Paivio, A. (1986). Mental Representations: A Dual Coding Approach. Oxford University Press.

learning_science.why: Vocabulary breadth spans a huge range, so presenting words near the child's current level yields the most information per item and reaches the individual ceiling efficiently.
learning_science.concrete_decision: A frequency staircase raises/lowers word rarity (Zipf band) after correct/incorrect answers to locate the lexical ceiling (M-VOCABLVL / M-DIFFREACH).
learning_science.source: Weiss, D. J. (1982). Improving measurement quality and efficiency with adaptive testing. Applied Psychological Measurement, 6(4), 473-492.

learning_science.why: For gifted screening, differences in print exposure or language background can masquerade as ability; leveling and lure design isolate the target construct.
learning_science.concrete_decision: Distractors are matched on frequency and tagged as phonological / thematic / category lures so error meaning (M-LURETYPE) is separated from motor or guess noise.
learning_science.source: Haladyna, T. M., & Downing, S. M. (2004). Construct-irrelevant variance in high-stakes testing. Educational Measurement: Issues and Practice, 23(1), 17-27.

new_measurements_proposed.name: Lexical frequency ceiling
new_measurements_proposed.usefulness_tail: Vocabulary breadth is one of the strongest, most stable verbal-ability correlates; the rarest word-frequency (Zipf) band a child reliably handles separates gifted lexical depth once common words ceiling. An adaptive staircase individualizes the frontier, making it less coachable than a fixed word list.
new_measurements_proposed.how_to_collect: Run an adaptive frequency staircase over frequency-tagged word items (receptive vocab, opposites/synonyms, context cloze); record the lowest-frequency (rarest) band answered correctly at criterion.
new_measurements_proposed.how_much_to_collect: >=15-20 adaptive vocabulary items spanning several frequency bands to localize the ceiling with acceptable error.

new_measurements_proposed.name: Distractor lure profile
new_measurements_proposed.usefulness_tail: Which class of distractor (phonological cousin, category/semantic cousin, thematic associate, surface match) pulls a child's errors reveals the grain of their semantic/relational discrimination; category-cousin near-misses at high difficulty indicate latent ability just below the cut, refining placement beyond right/wrong.
new_measurements_proposed.how_to_collect: Tag every distractor with a lure class; on each error log the lure class chosen; aggregate the per-child error-by-lure distribution.
new_measurements_proposed.how_much_to_collect: Every incorrect response; requires items built with a designed lure taxonomy; >=10-15 errors for a stable profile (pooled across verbal types).

tail_precision_rationale: Vocabulary ceiling is one of the cleanest verbal tail separators: once high-frequency words are trivial for a gifted child, only the rarest words discriminate. The frequency staircase drives each child to their personal lexical ceiling (M-VOCABLVL / M-DIFFREACH) instead of stopping at grade level, while lure-type analysis (M-LURETYPE) confirms that near-misses at ceiling are fine semantic discriminations (category cousin) rather than random taps, adding resolution exactly at the cut.
age_rationale: Point-to-picture receptive vocabulary needs no reading and only a single tap, so it works from K-1. It is retained through 4-5 with rarer words, but above 4-5 a pure picture-vocab task tends to ceiling and loses tail information for gifted readers, where meaning-in-context (Story Quest, Fill the Gap) carries more signal; hence 6-8 is excluded by design.

adaptive.content_range: Concrete high-frequency nouns/verbs (K-1) through low-frequency and abstract words depicted via small scenes (4-5); frequency-leveled by Zipf band.
adaptive.difficulty_levers: word frequency/rarity; abstractness (concrete object vs depicted action/attribute); semantic closeness of distractors; number of tiles (2->4->6); audio-only vs audio+scene.
adaptive.notes: Items auto-generated from a frequency-tagged word bank paired with an image library; parallel forms cloned by swapping same-frequency words and same-lure-class distractors.

engagement_hook: A safari photo hunt: each correct tap snaps a photo of the animal/thing into a sticker album, and rarer words earn shinier stickers, so climbing the vocabulary ladder is the reward.
construct_irrelevant_risks: Highest verbal risk is language background and print exposure (mitigated by audio prompts, frequency leveling, and dialect-neutral imagery); image ambiguity (mitigated by prototypical pictures per Rosch); motor mis-tap (large tiles, lock-to-confirm, revisions logged via M-REV); device audio quality (caption fallback + replay button).

name: Bridge Pairs
one_liner: See a top pair of pictures that go together, then pick the picture that makes the bottom pair go together the same way.
interaction: A 2x2 matrix: top-left -> top-right shows a relation (bird -> nest); bottom-left is given and bottom-right is blank with four picture choices below. The child taps a choice; an arrow animates the mapped relation and the tile locks. Young bands hear the relation frame; older bands use printed frequency-leveled word pairs.
self_teach: Ghost-hand demo (<10s): the top pair connects with a glowing arrow, an identical arrow starts from the bottom-left, and the hand taps the picture that completes the same arrow. One unscored warm-up (dog->puppy, cat->?) with an obvious relation runs before scoring.

learning_science.why: Analogy is aligning relational structure rather than surface features; young children reason relationally when the relation is familiar and depictable, letting us measure fluid verbal reasoning with almost no vocabulary.
learning_science.concrete_decision: Relations use concrete, cross-culturally familiar pairs (animal->home, object->function) shown as pictures, so the near-language-free relation carries the item.
learning_science.source: Gentner, D. (1983). Structure-mapping: A theoretical framework for analogy. Cognitive Science, 7(2), 155-170.

learning_science.why: Children as young as 3-4 solve a:b::c:d analogies when the relations are within their knowledge, so picture analogies validly bridge pre-readers to older verbal analogies.
learning_science.concrete_decision: K-1 uses picture relations; the identical shell swaps in printed frequency-leveled word pairs for 6-8, letting one type span all bands.
learning_science.source: Goswami, U. (1992). Analogical Reasoning in Children. Lawrence Erlbaum.

learning_science.why: Zero written instructions and a single mapped arrow keep working memory on the relation instead of on decoding the task.
learning_science.concrete_decision: The animated arrow externalizes the relation frame; there is no instructional text.
learning_science.source: Sweller, J. (1988). Cognitive load during problem solving: Effects on learning. Cognitive Science, 12(2), 257-285.

tail_precision_rationale: Because the relation, not vocabulary, carries the item, correct answers on multi-relation or abstract-relation analogies isolate fluid-verbal reasoning near the cut with minimal language confound. The distractor taxonomy (M-ERRTYPE: surface-match lure vs relational-reversal lure) reveals whether a near-miss reflects partial relational alignment (latent ability just under threshold) versus surface capture, and first-action latency (M-RTFIRST) separates reflective mappers from guessers at ceiling.
age_rationale: Picture analogies with familiar relations are solvable from K-1 (single tap, no reading). The same shell scales to 6-8 by increasing relational complexity and switching pictures to printed frequency-leveled word pairs; motor demand stays a single tap throughout.

adaptive.content_range: One concrete relation (animal->baby) up to abstract/double relations (tool->action->product) and printed word analogies across domains.
adaptive.difficulty_levers: relation abstractness; number of relations combined; surface similarity of distractors; picture vs printed-word stimuli; adding a second relational dimension.
adaptive.notes: AIG from a relation-typed pair bank; distractors auto-built as surface-match, relation-reversal, and associate lures.

engagement_hook: Build a glowing bridge between pictures: each correct pair snaps a plank into place and a character walks across; wrong planks wobble, right ones lock.
construct_irrelevant_risks: This is the near-language-free verbal option, so it is the anchor against language bias; residual risks are relation familiarity carrying culture (mitigated by universal relations and adaptive drop of low-fit items via M-CONSIST), surface-feature capture in young children (mitigated by the warm-up + arrow scaffold), reading load only in the 6-8 word mode (mitigated by frequency leveling + an audio option), and single-tap motor keeping motor noise low.

name: Club or Odd One
one_liner: Find the picture or word that belongs with a group, or tap the one that does not fit.
interaction: Three stimuli that share a hidden property sit in a club; four candidates appear below. In Belongs mode the child taps the candidate that joins the club; in Odd-One mode four items show and the child taps the one to eject. The choice animates in/out and locks. Audio names the items for pre-readers; older bands use frequency-controlled words.
self_teach: Ghost-hand demo (<10s): three fruits glow together, the hand taps the fourth fruit (it flies into the club) and pushes a shoe away. One unscored warm-up (three animals + one car) runs before scoring.

learning_science.why: Category membership is graded around prototypes, so measuring how a child groups items reveals concept formation independent of decoding.
learning_science.concrete_decision: Groups are built around clear taxonomic categories for young bands and thematic/abstract categories for older, with member typicality controlled.
learning_science.source: Rosch, E. (1975). Cognitive representations of semantic categories. Journal of Experimental Psychology: General, 104(3), 192-233.

learning_science.why: Choosing the odd item requires inducing the shared rule and testing candidates against it, which is core inductive reasoning.
learning_science.concrete_decision: Log which candidates are sampled/hovered (M-EXPLORE) to distinguish systematic from random rule search.
learning_science.source: Bruner, J. S., Goodnow, J. J., & Austin, G. A. (1956). A Study of Thinking. Wiley.

learning_science.why: Removing written instructions keeps limited working memory on the category rule, not on decoding the task.
learning_science.concrete_decision: The club metaphor and animation teach the response with no instruction text.
learning_science.source: Sweller, J. (1988). Cognitive load during problem solving: Effects on learning. Cognitive Science, 12(2), 257-285.

tail_precision_rationale: Distractors are built as competing-category lures (an item that fits a different but plausible rule). At the tail, choosing the target over a strong competing-category lure shows the child found the more specific/abstract shared rule; M-LURETYPE plus M-EXPLORE reveal whether high performers converge quickly on the correct rule while others sample widely, adding process resolution beyond accuracy at the cut.
age_rationale: Picture classification by taxonomic category is solvable at K-1; abstraction (function, thematic, superordinate) and printed-word items raise it to 6-8. A single tap throughout keeps motor demands flat.

adaptive.content_range: Concrete taxonomic categories -> abstract/superordinate and cross-domain word classes.
adaptive.difficulty_levers: category abstractness (perceptual -> taxonomic -> functional/abstract); member typicality; strength of the competing-category lure; picture vs word.
adaptive.notes: AIG from category-tagged banks; lures auto-selected from a sibling category to control near-miss meaning.

engagement_hook: A club-bouncer game: wave the right member in and bounce the impostor out; combos reward fast-correct choices without false ejections.
construct_irrelevant_risks: Category knowledge can reflect exposure/culture (mitigated by universal categories for young bands and adaptive drop of low-fit items via M-CONSIST); picture ambiguity (prototypical art); reading only in word mode at older bands (frequency-controlled list per the qbank); single-tap motor.

name: Spot the Silly
one_liner: Find what is silly or impossible in a picture or short story, and for older kids show why.
interaction: A scene or short scenario is presented (audio + picture for young; text for older). The child taps the impossible element (a fish riding a bike) and it highlights. For 4-5 and 6-8 a second step asks why it is silly, answered by picture/choice (young) or a short typed reason (oldest), scored for the identified violation as partial credit.
self_teach: Ghost-hand demo (<10s): a scene shows the sun wearing mittens; the hand taps the mittens and a giggle pop appears. One unscored warm-up (an upside-down umbrella catching rain) runs before scoring.

learning_science.why: Detecting an impossibility requires integrating each element against world knowledge; the speed and success of that integration index verbal reasoning and knowledge structure.
learning_science.concrete_decision: Items embed a single well-defined world-knowledge violation and the response is tapping the violating element, separating detection from expressive language.
learning_science.source: Kutas, M., & Hillyard, S. A. (1980). Reading senseless sentences: Brain potentials reflect semantic incongruity. Science, 207(4427), 203-205.

learning_science.why: Verbal Absurdities is a long-validated marker of verbal comprehension and reasoning in standardized batteries.
learning_science.concrete_decision: Keep the classic construct but replace spoken-explanation scoring with taps plus an optional short justification to reduce expressive-language load for young and ELL children.
learning_science.source: Roid, G. H. (2003). Stanford-Binet Intelligence Scales, Fifth Edition (SB5): Technical Manual. Riverside.

learning_science.why: Explaining why something is impossible requires building and checking a coherent mental model of the scenario, which is the deep-comprehension signal for the why step.
learning_science.concrete_decision: The why step is scored by inference depth (M-INFDEPTH), from naming the violation to explaining its consequence.
learning_science.source: Kintsch, W. (1988). The role of knowledge in discourse comprehension: A construction-integration model. Psychological Review, 95(2), 163-182.

new_measurements_proposed.name: Inference depth level reached
new_measurements_proposed.usefulness_tail: Comprehension discrimination at the tail is about inference layer, not literal recall; recording the deepest layer answered correctly (literal -> local/bridging inference -> global/thematic -> author's-purpose/evaluative) cleanly separates strong comprehenders who reach evaluative inference from those who plateau at literal.
new_measurements_proposed.how_to_collect: Tag each comprehension/absurdity/cloze probe with an inference-depth level; record the maximum level answered correctly at criterion within a passage/unit.
new_measurements_proposed.how_much_to_collect: >=4-6 probes spanning depth levels per passage/unit; several passages to stabilize the estimate.

tail_precision_rationale: The two-step design turns one item into a graded measure: detecting the anomaly (M-ACC) plus articulating the correct violation and its consequence (M-POLY, M-INFDEPTH). At the tail, gifted children not only spot subtle, plausibility-graded absurdities fast (M-RTFIRST) but explain the causal/logical reason, so inference-depth scoring separates saw it from understood why precisely where the cut sits.
age_rationale: Tap-the-silly picture works at K-1 (recognition only). The explanation step and text scenarios are added at 4-5 and deepened at 6-8; the pre-reader version needs no reading or expressive language.

adaptive.content_range: Obvious visual impossibilities -> subtle plausibility violations and multi-clause scenario absurdities.
adaptive.difficulty_levers: salience of the violation; number of plausible-but-fine elements (distractor density); picture -> audio -> text; required explanation depth.
adaptive.notes: Scene templates with a swappable violation slot; explanation rubric anchors define the partial-credit categories.

engagement_hook: A silly-detector meter that giggles and fills up when you catch the impossible thing; subtler absurdities are worth more giggles.
construct_irrelevant_risks: The why step adds expressive-language/writing load (mitigated by picture/choice justification for young bands, optional speech-to-text, and keeping typed reasons out of young bands); world knowledge can be cultural (mitigated by universal physical/biological violations); single-tap motor for detection.

name: Flip It
one_liner: Find the opposite, or the closest match, of a spoken or printed word.
interaction: A target is given (audio + picture for young; printed word for older). In Opposite mode the child taps the picture/word that means the reverse; in Match mode taps the closest-in-meaning option. The choice locks with a flip animation. A frequency staircase adjusts word rarity after each answer.
self_teach: Ghost-hand demo (<10s): a big elephant target shows; the hand taps the tiny mouse and a flip animation plays (big <-> small). One unscored warm-up (up/down arrows) runs before scoring.

learning_science.why: Judging antonymy/synonymy is comparing shared versus contrasting semantic features, probing depth of lexical-semantic representation beyond merely knowing a word.
learning_science.concrete_decision: Opposites use a single contrasting dimension for young items (size, height) and multi-feature contrasts for older; synonyms control shared-feature distance.
learning_science.source: Smith, E. E., Shoben, E. J., & Rips, L. J. (1974). Structure and process in semantic memory. Psychological Review, 81(3), 214-241.

learning_science.principle: Vocabulary as a reasoning/exposure proxy (Matthew effect)
learning_science.why: Depth and breadth of word-meaning relations predict verbal reasoning, but raw exposure must not be rewarded on its own.
learning_science.concrete_decision: Frequency-matched distractors and adaptive rarity ensure the score reflects semantic-relation reasoning (M-VOCABLVL) rather than simply having met the word.
learning_science.source: Stanovich, K. E. (1986). Matthew effects in reading. Reading Research Quarterly, 21(4), 360-407.

learning_science.why: Picture-opposite items let pre-readers show antonym reasoning without any print, verifying meaning across verbal and visual codes.
learning_science.concrete_decision: Young items are audio prompt + picture choices; printed words appear only from 4-5 up.
learning_science.source: Paivio, A. (1986). Mental Representations: A Dual Coding Approach. Oxford University Press.

tail_precision_rationale: Antonym/synonym items with frequency-matched lures push discrimination into fine semantic space; the adaptive rarity staircase locates the lexical ceiling (M-VOCABLVL) while lure analysis (M-LURETYPE) flags whether ceiling errors are near-synonym confusions (fine-grained, latent ability) versus associative captures, sharpening placement right at the gifted cut.
age_rationale: Concrete picture opposites (big/small, up/down, happy/sad) are within K-1 grasp with audio; abstract antonyms and nuanced synonyms with printed words extend to 6-8. Single tap; reading load only in the older word mode.

adaptive.content_range: Concrete perceptual opposites -> abstract antonyms and nuanced synonyms.
adaptive.difficulty_levers: word frequency; abstractness; opposite vs synonym mode; semantic distance of the lure; picture vs word.
adaptive.notes: Antonym/synonym pair bank tagged by frequency and semantic distance; parallel clones swap same-band pairs.

engagement_hook: A mirror world where tapping the opposite flips the scene (day -> night); Match mode magnetizes twins together.
construct_irrelevant_risks: Opposition/synonymy is highly language- and culture-loaded (the highest-bias verbal skill; mitigated by audio and picture mode for young, frequency leveling, and ELL-neutral concepts); abstract relations are hard to depict (older bands use words); single-tap motor; guessing controlled via M-CONSIST parallel items.

name: Do What I Say
one_liner: Listen to a spoken instruction and tap the picture(s) that satisfy every condition.
interaction: A grid of pictures/shapes (varying size, color, position) is shown. Audio gives a multi-condition direction (tap the small blue star that is above the tree). The child taps the matching cell(s); multi-step directions require an ordered sequence of taps; a replay button repeats the audio once. Taps lock on submit.
self_teach: Ghost-hand demo (<10s): audio plays the big red circle; the hand hovers each shape then taps the big red circle. One unscored warm-up (tap the yellow sun) runs before scoring.

learning_science.why: Comprehending increasingly complex spoken directions (embedded clauses, multiple constraints) is a validated index of receptive language and verbal working memory.
learning_science.concrete_decision: Directions scale from one attribute to multiple embedded spatial/relational constraints acting on a controlled picture grid.
learning_science.source: De Renzi, E., & Vignolo, L. A. (1962). The Token Test: A sensitive test to detect receptive disturbances in aphasics. Brain, 85(4), 665-678.

learning_science.why: Holding several conditions while scanning taxes updating; the maximum conditions integrated is a strong reasoning- and EF-linked signal.
learning_science.concrete_decision: An adaptive condition-count staircase yields an oral-direction span (M-ORALSPAN).
learning_science.source: Baddeley, A. (1992). Working memory. Science, 255(5044), 556-559.

learning_science.why: A spoken direction paired with a visual grid lets the child map language onto objects without any reading.
learning_science.concrete_decision: All directions are audio; all targets are pictures/shapes on the grid.
learning_science.source: Paivio, A. (1986). Mental Representations: A Dual Coding Approach. Oxford University Press.

new_measurements_proposed.name: Oral-direction condition span
new_measurements_proposed.usefulness_tail: The maximum number of simultaneous spoken conditions a child can integrate before dropping one is a sharp, near-language-neutral tail separator that jointly loads receptive language and verbal working memory; gifted children reliably cross-reference 4-5 embedded constraints.
new_measurements_proposed.how_to_collect: Adaptive condition-count staircase on following-oral-directions items; record the highest condition count satisfied on all constraints at criterion; log which single condition is dropped on near-misses.
new_measurements_proposed.how_much_to_collect: >=12-16 adaptive direction items across condition counts; report span plus the near-miss condition-drop pattern.

tail_precision_rationale: The adaptive condition-count staircase drives each child to the maximum number of simultaneous spoken constraints they can integrate (M-ORALSPAN / M-DIFFREACH), a sharp tail separator because gifted children hold and cross-reference 4-5 embedded conditions where others drop one. The tap sequence (M-PATH) shows whether they resolve constraints systematically, and near-misses (one condition dropped) are logged distinctly for fine placement.
age_rationale: One- or two-condition directions with pictures work at K-1; embedded-clause, multi-step directions extend to 6-8. No reading is required at any band (audio); motor is a tap or short tap sequence.

adaptive.content_range: Single attribute -> multiple embedded spatial/relational/conditional constraints and multi-step sequences.
adaptive.difficulty_levers: number of conditions; embedding/relational complexity; grid size; sequence length; single vs multi-tap; one replay allowed.
adaptive.notes: A grammar-templated direction generator over an attribute-tagged grid; auto-scored against the constraint set.

engagement_hook: A spell-caster vibe: each correct multi-condition tap casts a glowing rune, and longer instructions unlock bigger spells; it feels like Simon Says with magic.
construct_irrelevant_risks: Loads verbal working memory and can confound with pure reasoning (reported alongside WM; a single replay caps memory-only failure); audio clarity (caption fallback in the demo; production audio + replay); grid scanning adds visual-search/processing-speed variance (mitigated by untimed taps and modest grid sizes); language background (dialect-neutral, frequency-leveled direction wording).

name: Story Quest
one_liner: Follow a short story (listened to or read) and answer questions that require inferring who, why, and what happens next.
interaction: An illustrated narrative plays in segments (audio + picture for young; text passage for older). At pause points a probe appears with picture or text choices (who wanted what / why / what next / fact vs opinion); older bands add one short writing-to-sources constructed response scored by rubric as partial credit. Answers lock and the story continues.
self_teach: Ghost-hand demo (<10s): a two-panel scene plays (a child reaches for a cookie jar), a probe shows two faces (happy/sad); the hand taps the fitting face and the story continues. One unscored warm-up probe runs before scoring.

learning_science.why: Deep comprehension is building a coherent mental model, not recalling words; inference probes at pause points measure model quality directly.
learning_science.concrete_decision: Probes target the situation model (goals, causes, predictions) rather than verbatim recall; distractors match surface text to catch shallow readers.
learning_science.source: Kintsch, W. (1988). The role of knowledge in discourse comprehension: A construction-integration model. Psychological Review, 95(2), 163-182.

learning_science.why: Drawing local and global inferences distinguishes strong comprehenders beyond word reading.
learning_science.concrete_decision: Probes are graded from literal -> local inference -> global/thematic -> author's-purpose/evaluative (M-INFDEPTH).
learning_science.source: Cain, K., & Oakhill, J. (1999). Inference making ability and its relation to comprehension failure. Reading and Writing, 11(5), 489-503.

learning_science.why: Embedding probes inside an engaging narrative reduces the test anxiety and disengagement that bias comprehension scores.
learning_science.concrete_decision: Probes are woven into the quest with process logging (progress, persistence, hints) under an ECD evidence model.
learning_science.source: Shute, V. J. (2011). Stealth assessment in computer-based games to support learning. In Computer Games and Instruction (pp. 503-524). Information Age Publishing.

tail_precision_rationale: Comprehension tail signal comes from inference depth, not literal recall: M-INFDEPTH records the deepest layer (up to author's-purpose/evaluative) a child answers correctly, and M-POLY grades the constructed writing-to-sources response. Because probes escalate within one passage, a single unit yields a curve (M-PROG) that distinguishes readers who sustain deep inference from those who plateau at literal, exactly the discrimination needed at the gifted cut.
age_rationale: Listening comprehension with picture answers makes this valid at K-1 (no reading); the identical probe engine switches to read passages and constructed responses at 4-5 and 6-8. Constructed responses (writing load) are reserved for 6-8.

adaptive.content_range: Simple narrative with literal/one-step inference (young) -> multi-paragraph literary/informational text with global inference, fact/opinion, and author's purpose (6-8).
adaptive.difficulty_levers: passage length/complexity; required inference depth; listening vs reading; MCQ vs constructed; surface-match strength of distractors.
adaptive.notes: Quality passages are hard to fully auto-generate; probe sets and distractors are templatable over a human-curated passage bank.

engagement_hook: A branching quest where correct inferences unlock the next scene and collect story-gems; the child is a character advancing the plot, not taking a reading test.
construct_irrelevant_risks: Reading decoding can confound comprehension at older bands (mitigated by a listening mode and by separating decoding from inference via picture probes for young bands); constructed responses add writing load (6-8 only; rubric scores the idea not mechanics; optional speech-to-text); background knowledge (balanced topics and novel worlds); engagement gated by M-ENGAGE/M-PERSIST.

name: Fill the Gap
one_liner: Complete a sentence with the missing idea by picking the picture or word that best fills the gap.
interaction: A sentence is presented with a blank (audio with a beep at the gap plus pictures for young; a printed sentence with a blank plus word choices for older). The child taps the best option; it drops into the blank and the full sentence plays/reads back. Context-clue items require using the rest of the sentence; a scrambled-tiles variant asks the child to drag words into a meaningful order.
self_teach: Ghost-hand demo (<10s): the dog wants to ___ plays with pictures (bone / car / cloud); the hand taps the bone, it slots into the blank, and the sentence replays. One unscored warm-up runs before scoring.

learning_science.why: Filling a deleted element measures integration of syntactic and semantic context, a validated comprehension and language-proficiency index.
learning_science.concrete_decision: Gaps are placed so only contextual reasoning (not a single collocation) selects the answer; distractors fit locally but not globally.
learning_science.source: Taylor, W. L. (1953). Cloze procedure: A new tool for measuring readability. Journalism Quarterly, 30(4), 415-433.

learning_science.why: Using surrounding context to infer the right word is a hallmark of strong verbal reasoning and predicts vocabulary growth.
learning_science.concrete_decision: Higher bands include low-frequency target words recoverable only from context (M-VOCABLVL + M-INFDEPTH).
learning_science.source: Sternberg, R. J. (1987). Most vocabulary is learned from context. In M. G. McKeown & M. E. Curtis (Eds.), The Nature of Vocabulary Acquisition (pp. 89-105). Erlbaum.

learning_science.why: Oral sentence + picture completion lets pre-readers show sentence reasoning with no print.
learning_science.concrete_decision: Young items are audio sentence frames with picture options; printed cloze appears only from 4-5 up.
learning_science.source: Paivio, A. (1986). Mental Representations: A Dual Coding Approach. Oxford University Press.

tail_precision_rationale: Context-recoverable low-frequency targets make this a joint vocabulary-by-inference tail probe: M-VOCABLVL captures the rarity of words a child can pin from context and M-INFDEPTH captures whether they used global sentence meaning versus a local collocation. Parallel matched gaps (M-CONSIST) tighten the standard error right at the cut, and first-action latency (M-RTFIRST) flags reflective integration over guess-and-check.
age_rationale: Oral sentence completion with picture answers is valid at K-1 (no reading); printed cloze with context clues extends to 6-8. Single tap; reading load only in the older printed mode, offset by an audio option.

adaptive.content_range: Simple oral sentence + picture completion -> multi-clause cloze requiring global context and rare target words; a scrambled-order variant covers sentence arrangement.
adaptive.difficulty_levers: context distance (local vs whole-sentence); target word frequency; syntactic complexity; picture vs word; number of options.
adaptive.notes: Sentence-frame bank with gap slots; distractors auto-tagged local-fit vs global-fit; the scrambled-order variant supports sentence_arrangement.

engagement_hook: A missing-puzzle-piece snap: the right piece clicks into the sentence and the scene it describes comes alive (the dog actually chews the bone).
construct_irrelevant_risks: Sentence completion is language- and exposure-loaded (mitigated by audio for young bands, frequency leveling, and ELL-neutral frames); local-collocation shortcuts (mitigated by global-fit-only gaps with local-fit lures); reading load at older bands (audio option); single-tap motor.

name: Proof Hunt
one_liner: Answer a question about a short story, then tap the exact part that proves your answer.
interaction: A short passage is shown (audio + 3-4 comic panels for pre-readers; printed text split into tappable sentences for older bands). Step A: an inference/main-idea question appears with picture or text choices and the child taps an answer. Step B: the child taps the sentence(s) - or the comic panel - that is the evidence for that answer; selected text highlights and can be toggled off. Submit locks both parts. Scored as a two-part evidence-based selected response: full credit needs the right answer AND the right evidence.
self_teach: Ghost-hand demo (<10s): a two-panel scene plays (a child holds an empty lunchbox and frowns); the question shows two faces, the hand taps the hungry face, then glides to the empty-lunchbox panel and taps it so it glows as the 'proof'. One unscored warm-up runs before scoring.

learning_science.why: Requiring the child to locate the supporting evidence, not just pick an answer, forces them to ground inferences in the text and blocks lucky guessing, which is the modern standard for valid reading-comprehension measurement.
learning_science.concrete_decision: Every scored item is two-part: an inference answer plus a required text-or-panel evidence selection, scored together as partial credit (M-POLY).
learning_science.source: Smarter Balanced Assessment Consortium (2015). Evidence-Based Selected-Response and Technology-Enhanced Item Specifications for English Language Arts.

learning_science.why: Selecting correct evidence for an inference requires linking a conclusion back to the propositions that license it, exposing the coherence of the child's mental model rather than verbatim memory.
learning_science.concrete_decision: Answer distractors are surface-text matches while evidence distractors are true-but-irrelevant sentences, so only a coherent model selects both correctly.
learning_science.source: Kintsch, W. (1988). The role of knowledge in discourse comprehension: A construction-integration model. Psychological Review, 95(2), 163-182.

learning_science.why: Comprehension discrimination at the tail is about inference layer (literal -> bridging -> global -> author's purpose), so grading the depth of the question a child can support with evidence separates strong comprehenders.
learning_science.concrete_decision: Questions are tagged by inference depth and the deepest layer supported with correct evidence is recorded (M-INFDEPTH).
learning_science.source: Cain, K., & Oakhill, J. (1999). Inference making ability and its relation to comprehension failure. Reading and Writing, 11(5), 489-503.

tail_precision_rationale: Requiring evidence turns one comprehension item into a two-part partial-credit item (M-POLY): answer-only credit versus answer-plus-evidence separates children who truly grounded the inference from those who guessed. M-INFDEPTH records the deepest inference layer a child can support with correct evidence, and M-PATH (which sentences were tapped, in what order) plus M-ERRTYPE (chose a plausible-but-unsupported sentence vs an off-topic one) reveal near-misses that mark latent ability just under the cut.
age_rationale: A pre-reader version uses an audio story with 3-4 comic panels where 'evidence' is tapping the panel that shows the proof, so it works at K-1 with a single tap and no reading; from 2-3 up the passage becomes tappable printed sentences (highlight-the-proof), with longer text and deeper inference layers through 6-8. Reading load at older bands is offset by a read-aloud option.

adaptive.content_range: Two-panel picture stories with one-step inference (K-1) up to multi-paragraph literary/informational passages needing global or author's-purpose inference and multi-sentence evidence (6-8).
adaptive.difficulty_levers: passage length; inference depth (literal -> bridging -> global -> author's purpose); number of evidence sentences required; strength of the plausible-but-unsupported evidence lure; listening vs reading.
adaptive.notes: Passages are human-curated but question+evidence sets and lure sentences are templatable; parallel forms swap matched-difficulty passages.

engagement_hook: A detective mechanic: answering is 'making the accusation' and highlighting the evidence 'proves the case' - the passage flashes a magnifying-glass stamp and a 'Case Solved' badge only when answer and proof agree.
construct_irrelevant_risks: Reading decoding can confound comprehension at older bands (mitigated by a listen mode and by the picture-panel evidence version for young bands); highlighting UI could add motor/selection noise (large sentence hit-boxes, toggle-to-deselect, revisions logged via M-REV/M-PATH); background knowledge (balanced, novel-world topics); the evidence step is language-light (tap, not type) to protect ELL children.

name: Story Order
one_liner: Put the mixed-up parts of a story in the right order, then choose what happens next.
interaction: Three to six story parts appear scrambled - picture panels for pre-readers, sentence strips for older bands. The child drags them into a track to make the events make sense (temporal/causal order). When ordered, a 'what happens next?' probe offers picture or text choices; a 'why did it happen?' probe may also appear. Submit locks the order and the prediction. The order is auto-scored by how many pairs are in the correct relative order.
self_teach: Ghost-hand demo (<10s): three panels (plant a seed / water it / flower blooms) sit scrambled; the hand drags them into 1-2-3 order, then a 'next?' card shows a bee visiting and the hand taps it. One unscored warm-up (wake up / eat breakfast / go to school) runs before scoring.

learning_science.why: Reconstructing event order requires representing goals, causes, and consequences (story grammar); success indexes causal-temporal inference beyond word reading.
learning_science.concrete_decision: Panels/strips are ordered by causal necessity, not just clock time, so correct sequencing requires inferring cause-effect links.
learning_science.source: Stein, N. L., & Glenn, C. G. (1979). An analysis of story comprehension in elementary school children. In R. O. Freedle (Ed.), New Directions in Discourse Processing. Ablex.

learning_science.why: Predicting what happens next from a reconstructed sequence is forward causal inference, a hallmark of strong comprehenders and a probe standard tests rarely score interactively.
learning_science.concrete_decision: After ordering, a prediction probe and an optional 'why' probe are graded by inference depth (M-INFDEPTH) as partial credit.
learning_science.source: Cain, K., & Oakhill, J. (1999). Inference making ability and its relation to comprehension failure. Reading and Writing, 11(5), 489-503.

learning_science.why: A drag-to-order mechanic with picture panels teaches itself and lets pre-readers show causal reasoning with zero print, keeping working memory on the story logic.
learning_science.concrete_decision: K-1 uses wordless picture panels and large drag targets; no instructional text at any band.
learning_science.source: Sweller, J. (1988). Cognitive load during problem solving: Effects on learning. Cognitive Science, 12(2), 257-285.

tail_precision_rationale: Ordering yields graded credit (M-POLY: number of correctly ordered pairs / Kendall-tau), turning one item into many bits of information, and the prediction + why probes add M-INFDEPTH (causal vs surface). The drag log (M-PATH) plus efficiency (M-EFF: moves vs the minimum needed) and revisions (M-REV) separate children who plan the causal chain and place decisively from those who shuffle by trial-and-error, adding process resolution exactly at the cut.
age_rationale: Wordless three-panel picture sequencing with large drag targets is within K-1 motor/attention range; strip count, causal subtlety, and a shift to sentence strips (which also carries sentence_arrangement) raise it through 6-8. Dragging (not typing) keeps expressive-language and reading load low; a read-aloud option covers decoding at older bands.

adaptive.content_range: 3 wordless picture panels in obvious time order (K-1) up to 5-6 sentence strips ordered by causal necessity with a global 'why' inference (6-8).
adaptive.difficulty_levers: number of parts; time-order vs causal-order; similarity/interchangeability of parts; picture vs sentence strips; presence of prediction and 'why' probes.
adaptive.notes: Event-chain templates generate scrambles and near-order distractors; curated art/sentences per chain; parallel forms swap matched chains.

engagement_hook: A comic-strip studio: snap the panels into a filmstrip and it 'plays' the little movie when the order is right, then you guess the next frame - reordering feels like storytelling, not testing.
construct_irrelevant_risks: Drag precision is a motor demand (large targets, snap-to-slot, free reordering, M-REV logged so motor fumbles are not scored as errors); reading load only in the sentence-strip mode (audio option, picture mode for young); working-memory load of holding the chain (kept modest by limiting parts by band); culturally balanced, universal event chains.

name: Shades of Meaning
one_liner: Put near-meaning words (or pictures) in order from weakest to strongest along a meter.
interaction: Three to five cards that share a meaning but differ in intensity appear (pictures for pre-readers - e.g., faces from calm to furious, or a drip to an ocean; frequency-leveled words for older bands). The child drags each card onto a labelled gradient bar (a thermometer/ladder) from least to most; the two ends can be opposite poles (antonym anchors) with synonyms ranked between. Submit locks the arrangement; scoring is by rank correctness (adjacent order).
self_teach: Ghost-hand demo (<10s): three water pictures (drip / puddle / ocean) and a thermometer appear; the hand drags them onto the bar small-to-big and it fills up. One unscored warm-up (three faces: content / happy / thrilled) runs before scoring.

learning_science.why: Synonyms differ by degree along shared semantic features; ordering by intensity probes fine-grained depth of word knowledge that a binary same/opposite choice cannot detect.
learning_science.concrete_decision: Each item set varies on ONE controlled dimension (size, temperature, emotion intensity, brightness) so the ranking isolates nuance discrimination.
learning_science.source: Smith, E. E., Shoben, E. J., & Rips, L. J. (1974). Structure and process in semantic memory. Psychological Review, 81(3), 214-241.

learning_science.why: Knowing subtle gradations among near-synonyms marks deep lexical representation, which predicts verbal reasoning better than mere word recognition at the high end.
learning_science.concrete_decision: Rarer, more nuanced synonym sets are introduced as the child succeeds, locating a nuance ceiling (M-VOCABLVL).
learning_science.source: Nagy, W. E., & Scott, J. A. (2000). Vocabulary processes. In Handbook of Reading Research, Vol. 3 (pp. 269-284). Erlbaum.

learning_science.why: Picture gradients let pre-readers show intensity ordering with no print, verifying meaning across verbal and visual codes.
learning_science.concrete_decision: K-1 and 2-3 use picture cards (sizes, facial-expression intensity); printed words appear from 4-5 up.
learning_science.source: Paivio, A. (1986). Mental Representations: A Dual Coding Approach. Oxford University Press.

tail_precision_rationale: Rank ordering is graded (M-POLY by adjacent-pair correctness / rank correlation), so a near-miss (one adjacent swap) scores above a scrambled attempt, and M-ERRTYPE flags adjacent swaps (fine nuance, latent ability) versus gross misordering. The nuance-rarity staircase locates a depth-of-meaning ceiling (M-VOCABLVL) that keeps separating gifted children after common synonyms ceiling, and the placement log (M-PATH) plus repositions (M-REV) show decisive nuance judgment vs trial-and-error.
age_rationale: Ordering three picture cards by an obvious dimension is within K-1 grasp with large drag targets; word cards, longer sets (4-5), and subtler nuance extend to 6-8. Dragging keeps expressive load low; reading load appears only in the older word mode (audio labels available).

adaptive.content_range: 3 picture cards on one obvious perceptual dimension (K-1) up to 5 nuanced low-frequency synonyms between antonym poles (6-8).
adaptive.difficulty_levers: number of cards; closeness of the intensity steps; concrete perceptual vs abstract dimension; picture vs word; word frequency of the synonyms.
adaptive.notes: Gradient sets generated from intensity-tagged synonym scales; parallel forms swap same-band scales; off-dimension 'flat' distractor cards can be added.

engagement_hook: A word-thermometer that fills and changes color as the order gets right, giving a satisfying 'temperature rising' payoff for capturing shades of meaning.
construct_irrelevant_risks: Synonymy/intensity is language- and culture-loaded (mitigated by picture mode for young, frequency leveling, ELL-neutral dimensions like size/temperature); drag motor demand (large snap slots, free repositioning, M-REV logged); abstract dimensions are hard to depict (reserved for older word mode).

name: Meaning Match
one_liner: Connect all the words (or pictures) that mean the same - or the opposite - into pairs at once.
interaction: A small board shows several cards (pictures for young; frequency-leveled words for older). In Same mode the child taps two cards that mean nearly the same to link them; in Opposite mode they link antonym pairs. A drawn line connects a pair and locks with a chime; a wrong link buzzes and clears. The child links every pair to clear the board. A mode icon (equals vs arrows) shows which relation to make.
self_teach: Ghost-hand demo (<10s): six picture cards appear; the hand connects big<->small and hot<->cold with glowing lines (Opposite mode). One unscored warm-up board (three easy synonym pairs) runs before scoring.

learning_science.why: Deciding that two words share (synonym) or contrast (antonym) their core features probes the structure of lexical-semantic memory, and doing several at once indexes the breadth of relations a child can command.
learning_science.concrete_decision: Boards mix several synonym or antonym pairs plus a near-lure card so linking requires precise feature comparison, not rough association.
learning_science.source: Smith, E. E., Shoben, E. J., & Rips, L. J. (1974). Structure and process in semantic memory. Psychological Review, 81(3), 214-241.

learning_science.why: Fluent, consistent access to word-meaning relations distinguishes strong verbal reasoners; consistency (low RT variability) tracks ability better than peak speed.
learning_science.concrete_decision: The board rewards sustained correct linking; per-link RT and its variability (M-RTVAR) are logged and raw speed alone is never scored.
learning_science.source: Perfetti, C. A. (2007). Reading ability: Lexical quality to comprehension. Scientific Studies of Reading, 11(4), 357-383.

learning_science.why: A tap-to-connect mechanic with a clear relation icon self-teaches and keeps working memory on meaning relations, not on task rules.
learning_science.concrete_decision: One relation mode is active at a time with a visible equals/opposite icon; no instructional text.
learning_science.source: Sweller, J. (1988). Cognitive load during problem solving: Effects on learning. Cognitive Science, 12(2), 257-285.

tail_precision_rationale: Linking several pairs on one board yields many decisions per item, and the mispair log (M-LURETYPE: pulled by a near-synonym vs an associate vs an off-relation card) reveals the grain of a child's semantic discrimination. Consistency of correct linking (M-RTVAR) and efficiency (M-EFF: extra tries vs the minimum links) separate fluent tail performers from guess-and-check, while the rarity of the pairs cleared indexes a lexical-relation ceiling (M-VOCABLVL).
age_rationale: Holding several relations in mind and connecting multiple pairs adds working-memory and (for words) reading load beyond K-1; picture-supported boards work from 2-3, with word boards and rarer, subtler pairs through 6-8. K-1 antonym/synonym reasoning is carried by Flip It and Shades of Meaning, so this type starts at 2-3 by design.

adaptive.content_range: 3 picture antonym/synonym pairs (2-3) up to 5-6 nuanced low-frequency word pairs with a near-lure card (6-8).
adaptive.difficulty_levers: number of pairs on the board; synonym vs antonym mode; semantic closeness of the lure card; picture vs word; word frequency; optional time pressure.
adaptive.notes: Pair bank tagged by relation, frequency, and semantic distance; boards auto-assembled with a controlled lure; parallel forms swap same-band pairs.

engagement_hook: A connect-the-cards puzzle that clears the board with glowing links and a combo for a clean sweep with no wrong links - fast and game-like without penalizing careful players.
construct_irrelevant_risks: Antonymy/synonymy is highly language- and culture-loaded (mitigated by picture boards for younger, frequency leveling, ELL-neutral concepts, and starting at 2-3); multi-pair boards add working-memory load (kept modest by band-limited pair counts and reported so it is not read as pure vocabulary); reading load in word mode (audio labels); tap-to-connect keeps motor demand low and wrong links auto-clear (logged via M-REV, not scored as motor error).

name: Zoom In
one_liner: Hear a word and tap the exact thing - or part or detail - it names inside one busy picture.
interaction: A single rich illustration fills the screen; a speaker plays a target word (audio in production; play-button + caption in this demo). The child taps the matching object, PART, or attribute directly in the scene (e.g., 'trunk' on an elephant, 'crescent' in the sky); the tapped region highlights and locks. A 'tap all the ___' breadth variant lets the child tap every matching thing (e.g., every vehicle). Word rarity/precision adapts by a staircase after each answer. No printed words are read.
self_teach: Ghost-hand demo (<10s): a park scene shows; the speaker pulses on 'kite', and the hand glides up to the kite in the sky and taps it with a happy pop. One unscored warm-up ('dog' in the scene) runs before scoring.

learning_science.why: Mapping a spoken word to its referent with no expressive demand is the cleanest low-literacy measure of vocabulary knowledge; embedding the referent in a scene extends it to parts and attributes, not just whole objects.
learning_science.concrete_decision: Targets include objects, parts, and attributes within one scene, probing precise word knowledge a four-tile format cannot reach.
learning_science.source: Dunn, L. M., & Dunn, D. M. (2007). Peabody Picture Vocabulary Test, Fourth Edition (PPVT-4). Pearson.

learning_science.why: Vocabulary spans a huge range, so probing words near the child's level and escalating to rarer or more precise terms reaches the individual ceiling efficiently.
learning_science.concrete_decision: A frequency/precision staircase raises word rarity after correct taps to locate the lexical ceiling (M-VOCABLVL / M-DIFFREACH).
learning_science.source: Weiss, D. J. (1982). Improving measurement quality and efficiency with adaptive testing. Applied Psychological Measurement, 6(4), 473-492.

learning_science.why: In-scene search adds a visual-search component that could confound vocabulary, so timing and scene density are controlled and search behavior is logged separately.
learning_science.concrete_decision: Taps are untimed for scoring, scene clutter is banded, and pre-commit region sampling is logged (M-EXPLORE) to separate 'did not know the word' from 'still scanning'.
learning_science.source: Haladyna, T. M., & Downing, S. M. (2004). Construct-irrelevant variance in high-stakes testing. Educational Measurement: Issues and Practice, 23(1), 17-27.

tail_precision_rationale: Because targets extend to parts and attributes, the rarity/precision staircase drives each child to a personal lexical ceiling (M-VOCABLVL / M-DIFFREACH) that whole-object four-choice vocab tasks hit too early for gifted children. The 'tap all the ___' breadth variant yields hits and false alarms for a sensitivity index (M-DPRIME) separating precise knowers from over-tappers, and pre-commit region sampling (M-EXPLORE) with first-action latency (M-RTFIRST) distinguishes 'knew it instantly' from visual search.
age_rationale: Tapping a named object in a scene needs no reading and one tap, so it works from K-1; escalating to parts, attributes, and rare precise words extends it through 6-8. Scene density is capped for young bands to bound visual-search load; all prompts are audio.

adaptive.content_range: Common whole objects in an uncluttered scene (K-1) up to precise parts, attributes, and low-frequency terms in a denser scene (6-8).
adaptive.difficulty_levers: word frequency; object vs part vs attribute; scene clutter / number of plausible regions; single-tap vs 'tap all' breadth; semantic closeness of nearby foils.
adaptive.notes: Scenes are curated with tagged hotspot regions; word-to-region mappings and near foils are templatable; parallel forms swap same-frequency targets across matched scenes.

engagement_hook: A hidden-picture 'zoom and find' vibe: each correct tap zooms in with a camera-shutter pop and snapshots the detail into a field journal; rarer words fill rarer journal pages.
construct_irrelevant_risks: Language background and print exposure are the main verbal risks (mitigated by audio prompts, frequency leveling, dialect-neutral art); in-scene visual search can confound processing speed (untimed scoring, banded clutter, M-EXPLORE separates search from knowledge); image/region ambiguity (prototypical art, generous hit-boxes); motor mis-tap (large regions, lock-to-confirm).

name: Riddle Pics
one_liner: Hear a short clue about what a word means and tap the picture it describes.
interaction: Four picture tiles appear; a speaker plays a short spoken clue/definition instead of the bare word (e.g., 'the one you open to stay dry in the rain'); audio in production, play-button + caption in this demo. The child taps the matching picture and it locks with a pop. Clues get longer and more abstract as the child succeeds. No printed words are read and all four options stay pictures.
self_teach: Ghost-hand demo (<10s): four pictures show; the speaker plays 'the animal that says woof and wags its tail', and the hand glides to the dog and taps it. One unscored warm-up ('the yellow fruit a monkey loves') runs before scoring.

learning_science.why: Mapping a meaning description to a referent probes conceptual/definitional word knowledge and lowers the exact-label-retrieval barrier, widening who can show vocabulary depth (helpful for ELL and dialect differences).
learning_science.concrete_decision: The prompt is a spoken clue about meaning, not the target label, and every response is a picture, so no expressive language or reading is required.
learning_science.source: Dunn, L. M., & Dunn, D. M. (2007). Peabody Picture Vocabulary Test, Fourth Edition (PPVT-4). Pearson.

learning_science.why: A multi-clue riddle requires integrating several semantic features and eliminating near-misses, adding a light inference load that distinguishes deep from shallow word knowledge.
learning_science.concrete_decision: Higher bands use two-to-three-feature clues whose foils each satisfy only one feature, so only integrating all cues selects the target.
learning_science.source: Sternberg, R. J. (1987). Most vocabulary is learned from context. In M. G. McKeown & M. E. Curtis (Eds.), The Nature of Vocabulary Acquisition (pp. 89-105). Erlbaum.

learning_science.why: Escalating clue abstractness and target rarity reaches each child's vocabulary ceiling efficiently instead of stopping at grade level.
learning_science.concrete_decision: A staircase raises target-word rarity and clue abstractness after correct answers to locate the ceiling (M-VOCABLVL / M-DIFFREACH).
learning_science.source: Weiss, D. J. (1982). Improving measurement quality and efficiency with adaptive testing. Applied Psychological Measurement, 6(4), 473-492.

tail_precision_rationale: Definition clues let the rarity/abstractness staircase locate a vocabulary-depth ceiling (M-VOCABLVL / M-DIFFREACH) while sidestepping label-retrieval, so gifted conceptual knowledge shows even when the exact label is unfamiliar. Foils are tagged by lure class (category cousin, single-feature match, thematic associate) so M-LURETYPE / M-ERRTYPE reveal whether ceiling errors are fine feature confusions (latent ability just under the cut) or random taps, sharpening placement.
age_rationale: A one-clue spoken riddle with picture choices needs no reading and a single tap, valid from K-1; multi-feature, more abstract clues and rarer targets extend through 6-8. All prompts are audio with a replay; responses are always pictures.

adaptive.content_range: One-feature clues for common concrete words (K-1) up to multi-feature abstract clues for low-frequency words (6-8).
adaptive.difficulty_levers: target word frequency; number of features in the clue; clue abstractness (perceptual -> functional -> abstract); semantic closeness of foils; number of tiles.
adaptive.notes: Clue templates generated from a feature-tagged word bank; foils auto-selected to satisfy exactly one clue feature (single-feature lures); parallel forms swap same-frequency targets.

engagement_hook: A guessing-game 'riddle master' vibe: solving the riddle flips the picture with a sparkle and reveals the secret word said aloud, so kids feel like they cracked a code.
construct_irrelevant_risks: Clue wording can carry language/culture load (mitigated by frequency-leveled, dialect-neutral clues, audio delivery, and picture-only responses); listening comprehension of the clue adds a light load (kept short with a replay so it does not become a memory test); image ambiguity (prototypical art); single-tap motor with lock-to-confirm.

name: Word Links
one_liner: Figure out how the first word-pair goes together, then pick the word (or picture) that makes the second pair go together the same way.
interaction: A left pair A -> B is shown with a small relation icon (a same-meaning icon, an opposite icon, or part/whole, category, and function icons); C is given and its partner is blank with four picture or word choices. The child taps a choice; a rail animates the same relation from C to the chosen option and the tile locks. Young bands hear A, B, C and use picture choices; older bands read frequency-leveled printed words. A frequency staircase adjusts word rarity after each answer.
self_teach: Ghost-hand demo (<10s): the A -> B pair lights with its relation icon (hot, opposite, cold), an identical icon slides from C (up), and the hand taps the opposite word (down) so the rail glows to show the matched relation. One unscored warm-up (day / opposite / night) runs before scoring.

learning_science.why: Analogy is aligning relational structure, not surface features; making the shared relation explicit lets us measure relational reasoning with minimal vocabulary load.
learning_science.concrete_decision: Each item shows an explicit relation icon (same/opposite/part/category/function) so the child maps the relation, and antonym/synonym items are the simplest relation cases carried by the same shell.
learning_science.source: Gentner, D. (1983). Structure-mapping: A theoretical framework for analogy. Cognitive Science, 7(2), 155-170.

learning_science.why: Judging same- versus opposite-meaning is comparing shared and contrasting semantic features, probing the depth of lexical-semantic representation that underlies both synonyms/antonyms and word analogies.
learning_science.concrete_decision: Same-meaning and opposite relations reuse one relation-rail engine so antonyms_synonyms and verbal_analogy are assessed with a common, frequency-leveled item bank.
learning_science.source: Smith, E. E., Shoben, E. J., & Rips, L. J. (1974). Structure and process in semantic memory. Psychological Review, 81(3), 214-241.

learning_science.why: Word knowledge and relational subtlety span a huge range, so presenting relations near the child's level reaches the individual ceiling efficiently.
learning_science.concrete_decision: A SUBTLEX/Zipf frequency staircase raises word rarity and relation abstractness after correct answers to locate the lexical/relational ceiling (M-VOCABLVL / M-DIFFREACH).
learning_science.source: Weiss, D. J. (1982). Improving measurement quality and efficiency with adaptive testing. Applied Psychological Measurement, 6(4), 473-492.

tail_precision_rationale: Because an explicit relation icon carries the item, correct answers on abstract or low-frequency relations isolate relational-verbal reasoning near the cut with minimal vocabulary confound. The frequency staircase drives each child to a personal lexical/relational ceiling (M-VOCABLVL / M-DIFFREACH); lure tagging (M-LURETYPE: associate vs surface vs relation-reversal) shows whether ceiling errors are fine relational confusions (latent ability just under threshold) versus random taps; first-action latency (M-RTFIRST) separates reflective mappers from guessers; and matched parallel items (M-CONSIST) tighten the standard error right at the cut.
age_rationale: Picture relations with audio (same/opposite/category) are solvable at K-1 with a single tap and no reading; the identical relation-rail shell scales to 6-8 by raising relation abstractness and switching to printed frequency-leveled words. Motor demand stays one tap throughout.

adaptive.content_range: One concrete relation (hot/cold, dog/puppy) up to abstract or multi-step relations and low-frequency printed word analogies across domains.
adaptive.difficulty_levers: relation abstractness; word frequency (Zipf band); same/opposite vs part/category/function relation; semantic closeness of distractors; picture vs printed word.
adaptive.notes: AIG from a relation-typed, frequency-tagged word/pair bank; distractors auto-built as relation-reversal, associate, and surface-match lures; parallel forms swap same-band pairs.

engagement_hook: Lay glowing rails between words: each correct link snaps a rail into place and a little train rolls across; opposite links flip the scene (day to night) and same-meaning links magnetize twins together.
construct_irrelevant_risks: Word relations are language- and culture-loaded (the highest verbal-bias risk; mitigated by audio + picture mode for young bands, SUBTLEX/Zipf frequency leveling, and dialect-neutral concepts); abstract relations are hard to depict (older bands use printed words with an audio option); reading load only in the word mode (frequency leveling + read-aloud); single-tap motor with lock-to-confirm; guessing controlled via matched parallel items (M-CONSIST).

name: Relation Match
one_liner: See how one pair of words goes together, then pick the OTHER pair that goes together in the very same way.
interaction: A key pair is shown (audio + pictures for young; printed frequency-leveled words for older), for example bird -> nest. Below are three or four candidate PAIRS; the child taps the pair whose relationship matches the key pair's (bee -> hive), not one that is merely associated. The chosen pair links to the key with an animated relation arc and locks. This is relation classification (matching a relationship) rather than completing A:B::C:?.
self_teach: Ghost-hand demo (<10s): the key pair bird -> nest lights with an arc; the hand hovers each candidate pair, rejects dog -> bone (wrong relation), and taps bee -> hive so a matching arc glows. One unscored warm-up (key fish -> water; pick bird -> sky) runs before scoring.

learning_science.why: Selecting the pair that shares a relation is pure relational alignment with surface content varied, so it isolates relational reasoning from single-word vocabulary.
learning_science.concrete_decision: Candidate pairs are built so one shares the key relation while distractors share only an associate or surface link, forcing relation (not theme) matching.
learning_science.source: Gentner, D. (1983). Structure-mapping: A theoretical framework for analogy. Cognitive Science, 7(2), 155-170.

learning_science.why: Children move from matching on surface/associative similarity to matching on relational similarity; which basis a child uses is a graded index of relational maturity and reasoning.
learning_science.concrete_decision: Distractors include an associative lure (thematically related but wrong relation) so the response reveals whether the child matches relationally or associatively (M-LURETYPE).
learning_science.source: Gentner, D., & Rattermann, M. J. (1991). Language and the career of similarity. In Perspectives on Language and Thought (pp. 225-277). Cambridge University Press.

learning_science.why: Zero written instructions and a single animated relation arc keep working memory on the relationship rather than on decoding the task.
learning_science.concrete_decision: The relation arc externalizes the mapping and there is no instructional text; young bands use pictures with audio labels.
learning_science.source: Sweller, J. (1988). Cognitive load during problem solving: Effects on learning. Cognitive Science, 12(2), 257-285.

tail_precision_rationale: Matching relations across varied surface content isolates fluid relational-verbal reasoning at the cut. The lure taxonomy (M-LURETYPE / M-ERRTYPE: associate lure vs surface-match lure vs reversed-relation lure) reveals whether a near-miss reflects associative capture (surface reasoning) or a subtle relational confusion (latent ability just under threshold); candidate-sampling (M-EXPLORE) and first-action latency (M-RTFIRST) separate decisive relational matchers from those who compare pairs one-by-one, adding process resolution beyond accuracy.
age_rationale: Matching a familiar relation between picture pairs is within K-1 grasp (single tap, no reading, audio labels); raising relation abstractness and switching to printed frequency-leveled words extends it to 6-8. Motor demand is one tap throughout.

adaptive.content_range: One concrete relation among picture pairs (animal->home) up to abstract or double relations among low-frequency printed word pairs.
adaptive.difficulty_levers: relation abstractness; number of candidate pairs; strength of the associative lure; picture vs printed word; word frequency.
adaptive.notes: AIG from a relation-typed pair bank; distractor pairs auto-selected as associate, surface-match, and reversed-relation lures; parallel forms swap same-band pairs.

engagement_hook: A matchmaker game: draw a glowing arc between the two pairs that belong together the same way; the right match sparks and locks, an associate trap fizzles.
construct_irrelevant_risks: Relation familiarity can carry culture (mitigated by universal relations for young bands and adaptive drop of low-fit items via M-CONSIST); associative distractors must be calibrated so they mislead by reasoning, not by unfamiliarity; reading load only in the word mode (frequency leveling + audio option); single-tap motor keeps motor noise low.

name: Word Web
one_liner: Sort a set of words (or pictures) into bins around a hub word - Same-meaning, Opposite, and Does-not-belong.
interaction: A hub word sits in the center (audio + picture for young; printed frequency-leveled word for older) with several word/picture cards around it. The child drags each card (or taps a card then taps a bin) into one of three labelled bins: SAME meaning as the hub, OPPOSITE of the hub, or DOES NOT BELONG. A correct drop snaps with a chime; the board clears when every card is binned. Bins use labelled icons so no reading is needed to know the bins.
self_teach: Ghost-hand demo (<10s): hub 'happy'; the hand drags 'glad' into the SAME bin (it glows green), 'sad' into the OPPOSITE bin, and 'chair' into DOES NOT BELONG. One unscored warm-up (hub 'big': tall/huge vs tiny vs shoe) runs before scoring.

learning_science.why: Assigning each word to same/opposite/unrelated requires comparing shared and contrasting semantic features against a hub, probing the structure and depth of lexical-semantic memory more richly than a single two-choice item.
learning_science.concrete_decision: Each board mixes true synonyms, true antonyms, and an unrelated or near-associate lure so binning requires precise feature comparison, not rough association.
learning_science.source: Smith, E. E., Shoben, E. J., & Rips, L. J. (1974). Structure and process in semantic memory. Psychological Review, 81(3), 214-241.

learning_science.why: Sorting words around a hub is a categorization act; graded typicality of synonyms/antonyms lets us measure concept structure independent of expressive language.
learning_science.concrete_decision: Cards vary in typicality (near vs far synonym) and a competing-associate lure is included so the does-not-belong bin tests discrimination, not just knowledge.
learning_science.source: Rosch, E. (1975). Cognitive representations of semantic categories. Journal of Experimental Psychology: General, 104(3), 192-233.

learning_science.why: Placing near-synonyms versus mere associates marks deep lexical representation, which predicts verbal reasoning at the high end better than word recognition alone.
learning_science.concrete_decision: Rarer, more nuanced words are introduced as the child succeeds, locating a depth-of-meaning ceiling (M-VOCABLVL).
learning_science.source: Nagy, W. E., & Scott, J. A. (2000). Vocabulary processes. In Handbook of Reading Research, Vol. 3 (pp. 269-284). Erlbaum.

tail_precision_rationale: Binning several cards yields many decisions per item, so one board is graded (M-POLY by cards correctly binned) rather than pass/fail, and the mis-bin log (M-LURETYPE: a near-associate dropped into SAME, or a far synonym rejected as does-not-belong) reveals the grain of a child's semantic discrimination. The nuance-rarity staircase locates a depth-of-meaning ceiling (M-VOCABLVL) that keeps separating gifted children after common synonyms ceiling, and the drop sequence (M-PATH) plus re-bins (M-REV) show decisive judgment versus trial-and-error.
age_rationale: Holding a hub in mind while sorting several cards adds working-memory and (for words) reading load beyond K-1, so picture-supported boards start at 2-3, with word boards and rarer, subtler synonyms/antonyms through 6-8. K-1 antonym/synonym reasoning is carried by the single-choice Flip It and ordering-based Shades of Meaning; dragging keeps expressive load low.

adaptive.content_range: 3-4 picture cards around a concrete hub (2-3) up to 5-6 nuanced low-frequency word cards with a near-associate lure (6-8).
adaptive.difficulty_levers: number of cards; synonym/antonym typicality (near vs far); strength of the associate lure; picture vs word; word frequency.
adaptive.notes: Cards drawn from a hub-tagged synonym/antonym/associate bank; boards auto-assembled with a controlled lure; parallel forms swap same-band hubs.

engagement_hook: A web-building sort: fling each word to its glowing bin and watch a meaning-web light up around the hub; a clean sweep with no re-bins sparks a bonus.
construct_irrelevant_risks: Synonymy/antonymy is highly language- and culture-loaded (mitigated by picture boards for younger bands, frequency leveling, ELL-neutral hubs, and starting at 2-3); multi-card boards add working-memory load (kept modest by band-limited card counts and reported so it is not read as pure vocabulary); reading load in word mode (audio labels); drag motor demand (large snap bins, free re-binning, M-REV logged so fumbles are not scored as errors).

name: Silly Simon
one_liner: Listen to a spoken command and do it by tapping the right picture(s) - but if the command is impossible or silly, tap the giggle buzzer instead of obeying.
interaction: A small picture scene/grid is shown while audio speaks a command (play-button plus caption in this demo). Sensible, possible commands (tap the dog that is under the tree) are obeyed by tapping the matching picture(s) in order; impossible or absurd commands (put the elephant inside the acorn; make the fish ride a bicycle) must be rejected by tapping a that-is-silly buzzer instead of acting. Taps lock on submit and a replay button repeats the audio once. The number of conditions in obeyable commands and the subtlety of the absurdity both adapt up after success (an above-grade staircase).
self_teach: Wordless ghost-hand demo (<10s): audio plays a possible command and the hand taps the matching picture with a happy pop; then an impossible command plays and the hand pulls back and taps the giggle buzzer. One unscored warm-up (obey tap the sun; reject tap the color of Tuesday) runs before scoring.

learning_science.why: Comprehending increasingly complex spoken commands acting on objects is a validated index of receptive language and verbal working memory, and requiring the child to act isolates comprehension from expressive language.
learning_science.concrete_decision: Obeyable commands scale from one attribute to several embedded spatial and relational conditions on a controlled picture grid, and an oral-direction condition span is estimated (M-ORALSPAN).
learning_science.source: De Renzi, E., & Vignolo, L. A. (1962). The Token Test: A sensitive test to detect receptive disturbances in aphasics. Brain, 85(4), 665-678.

learning_science.why: Rejecting an impossible command requires integrating it against world knowledge, the classic Verbal Absurdities marker, but as a go/withhold decision it needs no spoken explanation, lowering expressive-language load for young and ELL children.
learning_science.concrete_decision: Impossible commands embed a single world-knowledge violation and are answered by withholding (tapping the silly buzzer), so absurdity detection is scored as a commission decision (M-COMM) rather than a verbal explanation.
learning_science.source: Kutas, M., & Hillyard, S. A. (1980). Reading senseless sentences: Brain potentials reflect semantic incongruity. Science, 207(4427), 203-205.

learning_science.why: A spoken command paired with a visual scene lets the child map language onto objects with no reading, keeping the item near-language-neutral for pre-readers.
learning_science.concrete_decision: All commands are audio, all obey-responses are picture taps, and a caption fallback plus one replay protect against audio and attention noise.
learning_science.source: Paivio, A. (1986). Mental Representations: A Dual Coding Approach. Oxford University Press.

tail_precision_rationale: Fusing obey-versus-reject makes one item carry two tail signals: the oral-direction condition span (M-ORALSPAN) drives each child to the maximum simultaneous spoken conditions they can integrate (gifted children hold 4-5 embedded constraints), while wrongly obeying an impossible command is a commission (M-COMM) that separates children who truly evaluate plausibility from those who act on autopilot. Error typing (M-ERRTYPE: dropped-one-condition near-miss versus obeyed-the-absurd) and low first-action-latency variability (M-RTVAR, M-RTFIRST) mark reflective, consistent integrators at the cut rather than merely fast responders.
age_rationale: One-condition obey/reject with pictures works at K-1 (single tap, no reading); embedded multi-condition commands and subtler, more plausible absurdities extend to 6-8. No reading at any band (audio plus one replay); motor is a tap or short tap sequence and the silly buzzer is a large fixed target.

adaptive.content_range: Single-attribute obey commands with obvious impossibilities (K-1) up to multi-condition embedded commands with subtle plausibility violations (6-8)
adaptive.difficulty_levers: number of conditions in obeyable commands; embedding and relational complexity; salience of the absurdity (obvious physical impossibility to subtle plausibility violation); ratio of obey to reject trials; grid size
adaptive.notes: A grammar-templated command generator over an attribute-tagged picture grid plus a swappable world-knowledge-violation slot; obey commands auto-scored against the constraint set and reject trials tagged by violation type; parallel forms swap same-band scenes.

engagement_hook: A Simon-Says with a twist: obey the real commands but catch Simon being silly - catching an impossible order fills a giggle-meter, so refusing to be tricked is the reward.
construct_irrelevant_risks: Loads verbal working memory alongside reasoning (one replay caps memory-only failure; reported with WM); world-knowledge absurdities can be cultural (mitigated by universal physical and biological violations and dialect-neutral, frequency-leveled command wording); audio clarity (caption fallback plus replay in the demo); a response bias toward always-obeying or always-buzzing is controlled by balancing obey and reject trials and reporting M-ERRTYPE; single large-target taps keep motor noise low.

name: Sentence Sense
one_liner: Drag the scrambled word cards into order to build the sentence that makes sense - not the silly one that breaks the rules of the world.
interaction: Word cards (picture-plus-word for young bands with audio labels; frequency-leveled printed words for older) appear scrambled on a rack. The child drags them into a track to form a sentence. The same words can form more than one grammatical order, but only one is sensible (the cat chased the mouse) while the other is absurd (the pizza ate the boy is impossible, or the mouse chased the cat is world-implausible in the framed scene); the child must build the sensible one. An optional second tap on the leftover silly reading marks why it is silly. Cards snap into slots, can be re-dragged (a revision), and lock on submit; scoring credits adjacent-pair order plus semantic plausibility.
self_teach: Ghost-hand demo (<10s): three scrambled cards (chased / cat / mouse with a the) are dragged into the cat chased the mouse and the scene plays it out; the reversed silly order wobbles and is rejected. One unscored warm-up (dog / the / barks) runs before scoring.
