learning_science.why: Arranging words into a grammatical sentence taps productive syntactic knowledge that comprehension-only items miss and that scales with syntactic complexity such as embedding and clauses.
learning_science.concrete_decision: Cards are arranged into a track and scored on word order, with complexity raised by adding clauses rather than rare words.
learning_science.source: Semel, E., Wiig, E. H., & Secord, W. A. (2003). Clinical Evaluation of Language Fundamentals, Fourth Edition (CELF-4): Sentence Assembly. Pearson.

learning_science.why: Choosing the sensible ordering over a grammatical-but-absurd one forces integration of the sentence against world knowledge, the Verbal Absurdities construct, so syntax and meaning are jointly probed.
learning_science.concrete_decision: Each item admits a grammatical absurd ordering as a lure so only a child who checks plausibility (not just grammar) scores full credit; the absurd reading is tagged for M-ERRTYPE.
learning_science.source: Kutas, M., & Hillyard, S. A. (1980). Reading senseless sentences: Brain potentials reflect semantic incongruity. Science, 207(4427), 203-205.

learning_science.why: A drag-to-order mechanic with a played-out scene self-teaches and keeps working memory on sentence logic, not on task instructions or decoding.
learning_science.concrete_decision: K-1 and 2-3 use picture-plus-audio cards and large drag targets with no instructional text; the assembled sentence is animated so meaning is verified visually.
learning_science.source: Sweller, J. (1988). Cognitive load during problem solving: Effects on learning. Cognitive Science, 12(2), 257-285.

tail_precision_rationale: Ordering yields graded credit (M-POLY by adjacent-pair correctness), turning one item into many bits, while the plausibility contrast adds inference depth (M-INFDEPTH: did the child reject a grammatical-but-absurd reading) that pure arrangement misses. The drag log (M-PATH) and re-drags (M-REV) separate decisive planners from shufflers, and M-ERRTYPE distinguishes a grammatical-but-silly ordering (semantic near-miss, latent ability) from an ungrammatical scramble, sharpening placement at the cut.
age_rationale: Arranging three picture-plus-audio cards is within 2-3 reach (large drag targets, no reading); printed word cards, longer sentences, added clauses, and subtler plausibility violations extend to 6-8. K-1 word-order building is heavier than a single tap so it is carried by tap-based verbal types and this type starts at 2-3 by design; dragging (not typing) keeps expressive load low.

adaptive.content_range: 3 picture-plus-audio cards forming a simple SVO sentence (2-3) up to 6-8 word printed cards forming multi-clause sentences with a grammatical-but-absurd lure (6-8)
adaptive.difficulty_levers: number of cards; syntactic complexity (SVO to embedded clauses); closeness of the absurd ordering to the sensible one; picture-plus-audio versus printed word; word frequency leveled so rare vocabulary does not confound syntax
adaptive.notes: Sentence frames generate scrambles plus a grammatical-but-implausible lure ordering; distractor orderings tagged ungrammatical versus grammatical-absurd; parallel forms swap same-band frames and same-frequency words.

engagement_hook: A word-builder where snapping the cards into the sensible order makes the scene come alive and act it out, while the silly order makes a goofy impossible cartoon - so getting it right is the funny payoff.
construct_irrelevant_risks: Sentence building is language- and exposure-loaded (mitigated by picture-plus-audio cards for young bands, frequency leveling so syntax not rare vocabulary carries difficulty, and ELL-neutral frames); world-knowledge plausibility can be cultural (universal physical and biological scenarios); drag motor demand (large snap slots, free re-dragging, M-REV logged so fumbles are not scored as errors); reading load only in the older printed mode (audio labels available).

name: Build-It Buddy
one_liner: Listen to step-by-step spoken directions and build the picture by dragging, placing, and coloring the pieces so it matches what was described.
interaction: An empty canvas plus a tray of pieces (shapes, animals, colors) is shown while audio gives a multi-step construction direction (put the red square in the top corner, then put a star under it, then color the tree green). The child performs each step by dragging a piece to a location, placing it, or tapping a color; a replay repeats the audio once. Unlike selection tasks the child constructs the arrangement from scratch. Steps lock on submit and are auto-scored against the described end-state as partial credit; the number of steps and embedded conditions adapt up after success (an above-grade span staircase).
self_teach: Wordless ghost-hand demo (<10s): audio gives a two-step direction and the hand drags a red circle to the box then puts a star on top, matching a briefly shown target. One unscored warm-up (put the sun in the sky) runs before scoring.

learning_science.why: Executing multi-step spoken directions that place and modify objects (put the red circle on the green square) is a validated receptive-language and verbal-working-memory index, and construction rather than selection removes recognition shortcuts.
learning_science.concrete_decision: Directions require building an arrangement from an empty canvas, scored step-by-step against the end-state, with an adaptive step and condition count (M-ORALSPAN, M-DIFFREACH).
learning_science.source: De Renzi, E., & Vignolo, L. A. (1962). The Token Test: A sensitive test to detect receptive disturbances in aphasics. Brain, 85(4), 665-678.

learning_science.why: Holding an ordered set of construction steps while executing them taxes updating and sequencing, a strong reasoning- and executive-linked signal.
learning_science.concrete_decision: Steps are delivered in one spoken pass with a single replay so the maximum ordered steps executed indexes span rather than re-listening.
learning_science.source: Baddeley, A. (1992). Working memory. Science, 255(5044), 556-559.

learning_science.why: A spoken direction paired with a manipulable visual canvas lets the child map language onto action with no reading, keeping the task near-language-neutral for pre-readers.
learning_science.concrete_decision: All directions are audio and all responses are drag/place/color actions on pictures; a caption fallback and replay protect against audio and attention noise.
learning_science.source: Paivio, A. (1986). Mental Representations: A Dual Coding Approach. Oxford University Press.

tail_precision_rationale: Construction turns one direction into a graded, multi-step item: partial credit (M-POLY) for steps satisfied plus the adaptive oral-direction step/condition span (M-ORALSPAN, M-DIFFREACH) drive each child to the maximum ordered spoken constraints they can hold and execute (a sharp tail separator because gifted children carry 4-5 embedded steps). The action log (M-PATH) shows whether they build systematically in the described order, and re-placements (M-REV) separate decisive builders from trial-and-error at the cut.
age_rationale: A one- or two-step build with large pieces is within K-1 motor and attention range; more steps, embedded conditions, and color/relational modifiers extend to 6-8. No reading at any band (audio plus one replay); drag/place/color on large targets keeps motor demand modest and revisions are logged so fumbles are not scored as comprehension errors.

adaptive.content_range: One- or two-step placements of large pieces (K-1) up to multi-step directions with embedded spatial, relational, and color conditions (6-8)
adaptive.difficulty_levers: number of steps; embedded conditions per step; relational and spatial complexity; piece count on the tray; single replay allowed
adaptive.notes: A grammar-templated construction-direction generator over a tagged piece/canvas library; each step auto-scored against the target end-state; parallel forms swap same-band pieces and layouts.

engagement_hook: A build-along craft game where following the spoken plan makes a little scene assemble itself piece by piece; finishing a long plan reveals a completed picture like following a treasure map.
construct_irrelevant_risks: Loads verbal working memory alongside comprehension (one replay caps memory-only failure; reported with WM and separated from motor via M-REV/M-PATH); drag precision is a motor demand (large snap targets, place-not-type); audio clarity (caption fallback plus replay in the demo); language background (dialect-neutral, frequency-leveled direction wording); construction adds a light visual-planning load kept modest by capped piece counts per band.

name: Word Train
one_liner: Drag the scrambled word cars onto the train track in the right order to build one correct, meaningful sentence.
interaction: Scrambled word cars sit on a platform (picture-plus-audio word cars for young bands; frequency-leveled printed words for older). The child drags them onto a track to form a grammatical sentence; the engine plays the sentence aloud when the order is meaningful. A recognition variant instead offers four candidate orderings and the child taps the correct one. Syntactic complexity rises with success (simple subject-verb-object up to embedded clauses) while word frequency is leveled so rare vocabulary never carries difficulty; cars re-drag freely (a revision) and lock on submit, scored by adjacent-pair and whole-order correctness.
self_teach: Ghost-hand demo (<10s): three scrambled cars (runs / the / dog) are dragged into the dog runs and the train chugs off reading it aloud. One unscored warm-up (a / nap / cat / the with an audio target) runs before scoring.

learning_science.why: Ordering words into a grammatical sentence taps productive syntactic competence that recognition items miss, and syntactic difficulty (clauses, embedding) provides a high ceiling for able children.
learning_science.concrete_decision: Cars are arranged on a track and scored on word order, with difficulty raised by syntactic structure rather than rare vocabulary.
learning_science.source: Semel, E., Wiig, E. H., & Secord, W. A. (2003). Clinical Evaluation of Language Fundamentals, Fourth Edition (CELF-4): Sentence Assembly. Pearson.

learning_science.why: Building complex (especially embedded) sentences loads verbal working memory, and individual differences in that capacity separate strong from average syntactic processors.
learning_science.concrete_decision: Complexity is scaled by embedding depth and clause count, and the highest structure a child orders correctly is recorded (M-DIFFREACH).
learning_science.source: King, J., & Just, M. A. (1991). Individual differences in syntactic processing: The role of working memory. Journal of Memory and Language, 30(5), 580-602.

learning_science.why: If rare words carried difficulty the task would measure vocabulary and print exposure, not syntax; leveling word frequency isolates the arrangement construct and lowers ELL bias.
learning_science.concrete_decision: Words are drawn from the child's frequency band via a Zipf staircase (M-VOCABLVL) and audio labels are provided so decoding does not gate syntax.
learning_science.source: Weiss, D. J. (1982). Improving measurement quality and efficiency with adaptive testing. Applied Psychological Measurement, 6(4), 473-492.

tail_precision_rationale: Word order is scored as graded credit (M-POLY by adjacent-pair correctness / Kendall tau), so one item yields many bits and near-misses (one transposition) score above scrambles. The highest syntactic structure ordered correctly (M-DIFFREACH) is an above-grade ceiling index, efficiency versus the minimum moves (M-EFF) and the drag path (M-PATH) separate planful builders from trial-and-error, and frequency leveling (M-VOCABLVL) guarantees the signal is syntax, not rare-word knowledge, right at the cut.
age_rationale: Ordering three picture-plus-audio word cars is within 2-3 reach with large drag targets and no reading; printed words, longer sentences, and embedded clauses extend to 6-8. K-1 multi-card ordering exceeds a single tap so it is carried by tap-based verbal types; dragging (not typing) keeps expressive load low and a read-aloud option offsets decoding at older bands.

adaptive.content_range: 3 picture-plus-audio cars forming a simple subject-verb sentence (2-3) up to 7-plus printed cars forming multi-clause sentences (6-8)
adaptive.difficulty_levers: number of cars; syntactic complexity (SVO to embedded and relative clauses); distractor orderings in the recognition variant; picture-plus-audio versus printed word; frequency band of the words
adaptive.notes: Sentence frames generate scrambles and near-order distractors; word frequency is a native staircase and syntactic templates give unlimited matched parallel forms.

engagement_hook: A train-building game where the word cars only chug away once the sentence is in the right order; longer, fancier sentences pull a longer, cooler train.
construct_irrelevant_risks: Sentence arrangement is language- and exposure-loaded (mitigated by picture-plus-audio cars for young bands, frequency leveling so syntax not rare vocabulary carries difficulty via M-VOCABLVL, and ELL-neutral frames); reading load only in the older printed mode (audio labels and read-aloud); drag motor demand (large snap slots, free re-dragging so fumbles are not scored as errors); working-memory load of holding the target sentence is kept modest by band-limited length.

name: Finish the Sentence
one_liner: Hear or read a sentence that stops partway - often right after a joining word like because, so, but, or if - and tap the ending that best completes it.
interaction: A friendly parrot speaks a sentence stem that trails off and freezes (audio plus a beep at the gap for young bands; a printed stem, and at higher bands a short context passage, for older bands). Three or four ending options appear below: picture tiles for pre-readers, frequency-leveled words or short phrases for older bands. The child taps the ending; it snaps onto the sentence, the parrot reads the whole completed sentence back, and the little scene acts it out. One ending is correct, one is a local-associate lure (fits a nearby word but not the whole idea or the joining word), and one is a logic-reversal lure (ignores the because/so/but). Answers lock on submit and a replay button repeats the stem once. Connective type, context distance, and target-word rarity adapt up after success.
self_teach: Wordless ghost-hand demo (<10s): the stem 'The plant grew tall because ___' plays with three pictures (sun-and-water / a hat / a car); the hand glides to sun-and-water, it snaps into the sentence, and the parrot finishes the sentence as the plant grows. Then one unscored warm-up ('I opened my umbrella because ___') runs with any answer accepted before scoring begins.

learning_science.why: Using a connective (because, so, but, if, when) to choose an ending forces the child to represent the logical relation between clauses, a comprehension skill beyond local word association that rises steeply with ability.
learning_science.concrete_decision: Stems are built around a target connective and the correct ending satisfies that relation while a logic-reversal lure satisfies the clause locally but violates the connective, so only relational completion scores.
learning_science.source: Cain, K., & Nash, H. M. (2011). The influence of connectives on young readers' processing and comprehension of text. Journal of Educational Psychology, 103(2), 429-441.

learning_science.why: Completing a trailing sentence requires building a coherent situation model and drawing a bridging/predictive inference to what must come next, the deep-comprehension signal rather than verbatim matching.
learning_science.concrete_decision: Endings are scored by inference depth (M-INFDEPTH): a literal collocation completion versus a causal/conditional completion that uses whole-sentence meaning.
learning_science.source: Kintsch, W. (1988). The role of knowledge in discourse comprehension: A construction-integration model. Psychological Review, 95(2), 163-182.

learning_science.why: An oral sentence stem paired with picture endings lets pre-readers show sentence-completion reasoning with no print, verifying meaning across verbal and visual codes.
learning_science.concrete_decision: Young items are audio stems with picture endings; printed stems and word/phrase endings appear only from 4-5 up, with an audio option retained.
learning_science.source: Paivio, A. (1986). Mental Representations: A Dual Coding Approach. Oxford University Press.

learning_science.why: Sentence completion confounds reasoning with word rarity unless target difficulty is individualized, so leveling ending words by frequency isolates the completion construct and lowers ELL/exposure bias.
learning_science.concrete_decision: A SUBTLEX/Zipf frequency staircase raises ending-word rarity after correct answers to locate the vocabulary-in-context ceiling (M-VOCABLVL) instead of stopping at grade level.
learning_science.source: Weiss, D. J. (1982). Improving measurement quality and efficiency with adaptive testing. Applied Psychological Measurement, 6(4), 473-492.

tail_precision_rationale: Because a connective or strong context carries the item, correct endings on subtle causal/conditional stems isolate relational verbal comprehension at the cut with minimal vocabulary confound. M-INFDEPTH records whether the child completed by local collocation or by whole-sentence causal/conditional meaning; M-LURETYPE and M-ERRTYPE reveal whether ceiling errors are local-associate captures versus logic-reversal confusions (a fine relational near-miss that marks latent ability just under threshold); the frequency staircase drives each child to a personal vocabulary-in-context ceiling (M-VOCABLVL); and first-action latency (M-RTFIRST) separates reflective integrators from guess-and-check.
age_rationale: An oral stem with picture endings and a single tap is valid at K-1 (no reading); printed trailing completions with explicit connectives, then context-passage completions with rarer context-recoverable words, extend it through 6-8. Reading load appears only in the older printed mode and is offset by an audio option; motor stays a single tap throughout.

adaptive.content_range: Simple oral stem plus picture ending on an everyday event (K-1) up to multi-clause printed completions gated by subtle connectives and short context passages with low-frequency, context-recoverable target words (6-8).
adaptive.difficulty_levers: connective type (and -> because/so -> but/although -> if/unless); context distance (local phrase vs whole-sentence vs prior-sentence context); target-word frequency (Zipf band); number of options; picture vs word/phrase endings.
adaptive.notes: Stem bank with a tagged connective slot and a frequency-tagged ending bank; endings auto-labeled correct / local-associate lure / logic-reversal lure; parallel forms swap same-connective stems and same-frequency endings.

engagement_hook: A chatty parrot that gets stuck mid-sentence and freezes in the air; tapping the right ending un-freezes it so it happily finishes the sentence and the little scene springs to life.
construct_irrelevant_risks: Sentence completion is language- and exposure-loaded (mitigated by audio stems and picture endings for young bands, SUBTLEX/Zipf frequency leveling, and ELL-neutral, dialect-neutral frames); a local-collocation shortcut can bypass reasoning (mitigated by endings that fit locally but violate the connective/whole-sentence meaning, tagged for M-LURETYPE); reading load only in the older printed mode (audio option and read-aloud); single-tap motor with lock-to-confirm keeps motor noise low.

name: Sorting Robot
one_liner: Watch a robot drop a few example pictures or words into its IN bin or OUT bin, figure out the hidden category rule, then sort new items IN or OUT yourself.
interaction: A friendly robot has a green IN bin and a red OUT bin. It first demonstrates by dropping two or three labeled examples - positive examples fall IN, negative examples fall OUT - revealing a hidden semantic category (for example, animals go IN and non-animals go OUT). Then new item cards are handed to the child one at a time; the child taps IN or OUT (or drags the card into a bin). An optional 'peek' lets the child test one example to see where the robot files it (a scored hint). Correct sorts snap with a chime and the robot's happy meter fills; the round ends after a fixed set. Audio names each item for pre-readers; older bands use frequency-leveled printed words and more abstract, superordinate, or functional categories. This is category-rule induction from examples, not picking a fourth member or ejecting an odd one.
self_teach: Wordless ghost-hand demo (<10s): the robot drops a dog IN, an apple OUT, and a cat IN (the hidden rule is 'animals'); a new fish card appears and the hand taps the IN bin so it snaps in. Then one unscored warm-up round (hidden rule 'round things') runs with feedback before scoring begins.

learning_science.why: Inducing a category from positive and negative examples and testing candidates against the inferred rule is core inductive classification, exposing concept formation rather than mere recognition of a named group.
learning_science.concrete_decision: Each round hides one semantic rule; the demonstrated examples are the positive/negative evidence and the child's sorts of new items reveal the induced rule; the test sequence is logged (M-EXPLORE).
learning_science.source: Bruner, J. S., Goodnow, J. J., & Austin, G. A. (1956). A Study of Thinking. Wiley.

learning_science.why: Semantic categories are organized around prototypes with graded membership, so using near-boundary exemplars probes the structure and precision of a child's concepts independent of expressive language.
learning_science.concrete_decision: Test items include clear central members plus near-boundary and competing-category lures so correct sorting requires precise category boundaries; young bands use universal, prototypical picture categories.
learning_science.source: Rosch, E. (1975). Cognitive representations of semantic categories. Journal of Experimental Psychology: General, 104(3), 192-233.

learning_science.why: How quickly a child converges on the hidden rule from feedback is a dynamic-assessment signal (learning rate) that adds tail validity beyond a static accuracy score and resists coaching.
learning_science.concrete_decision: Trials-to-criterion and the reduction in the viable-rule space per sort are scored as hypothesis-search efficiency (M-HYP), and optional peeks are logged (M-HINT) so hint-free fast induction is credited more.
learning_science.source: Grigorenko, E. L., & Sternberg, R. J. (1998). Dynamic testing. Psychological Bulletin, 124(1), 75-111.

tail_precision_rationale: Rule induction turns one classification round into a learning curve: M-HYP (trials-to-criterion / viable-rule-space reduction) captures how fast a child infers the hidden category, a dynamic-assessment tail separator beyond static accuracy, while M-EXPLORE and M-HINT distinguish systematic testers from guessers and credit hint-free induction. M-DIFFREACH escalates category abstractness (perceptual -> taxonomic -> functional/superordinate) to the child's edge, and M-ERRTYPE flags boundary near-misses (fine category discrimination, latent ability just under the cut) versus random misfiles.
age_rationale: IN/OUT sorting of obvious picture categories with audio labels and a single tap is within K-1 reach; abstract, superordinate, and functional categories with printed frequency-leveled words extend it through 6-8. No reading at young bands (audio); the response is a single tap or a large-target drag, and the demonstrated examples stay on screen so working-memory load of the rule is kept modest.

adaptive.content_range: Concrete taxonomic categories such as animals vs non-animals (K-1) up to abstract/superordinate and functional or cross-domain word categories (6-8).
adaptive.difficulty_levers: category abstractness (perceptual -> taxonomic -> functional/superordinate); closeness of boundary exemplars and competing-category lures; number of demonstrated examples before testing; picture vs printed word; word frequency (Zipf band).
adaptive.notes: AIG from category-tagged picture/word banks; positive and negative demonstration exemplars plus near-boundary and competing-category lures auto-selected; parallel forms swap same-abstractness categories and same-frequency words.

engagement_hook: A friendly robot that is 'thinking' of a secret rule; cracking the rule and feeding it the right items fills its happy meter and makes it beep with delight, so figuring out the robot's secret is the game.
construct_irrelevant_risks: Category knowledge can reflect exposure and culture (mitigated by universal, prototypical categories and audio-plus-picture for young bands, frequency leveling for words, and dropping low-fit items via matched parallels); reading load only in the word mode (frequency leveling plus audio labels); single-tap or large-target drag keeps motor noise low; the on-screen demonstration examples cap the working-memory load so the task measures induction, not memory.

name: Real or Impossible?
one_liner: For each short scene, decide whether it could really happen or could never happen, sending it through the Real door or the giggle Impossible door.
interaction: One short scene or statement is presented at a time (audio plus picture for young bands; printed text for older). The child taps a big green check 'Could really happen' door or a giggling red 'Could never happen' door. Several scenes stream by: some are perfectly plausible, others contain a single world-knowledge impossibility. On a subset (older bands) a quick 'sure / not sure' confidence tap follows the verdict. At higher bands a set shows several plausible scenes with exactly one subtly-impossible scene to catch. Verdicts lock on submit and a replay repeats the audio once. The design balances real and impossible scenes so a yes-or-no bias is separated from true detection.
self_teach: Wordless ghost-hand demo (<10s): a scene of a dog barking plays and the hand taps the green Real door with a nod; then a scene of a cat driving a bus plays and the hand pulls back and taps the giggle Impossible door. Then one unscored warm-up scene runs with either answer accepted before scoring begins.

learning_science.why: Judging whether a scene is possible requires integrating it against world knowledge, the classic Verbal Absurdities marker, but framed as a possible/impossible verdict it needs no spoken explanation, lowering expressive-language load for young and ELL children.
learning_science.concrete_decision: Each impossible scene embeds a single well-defined world-knowledge violation and is answered by a possible/impossible verdict rather than a verbal explanation.
learning_science.source: Kutas, M., & Hillyard, S. A. (1980). Reading senseless sentences: Brain potentials reflect semantic incongruity. Science, 207(4427), 203-205.

learning_science.why: A yes/no plausibility judgment conflates true detection with response bias, so separating sensitivity from bias prevents scoring a cautious child and a yes-biased guesser alike near the cut.
learning_science.concrete_decision: Real and impossible scenes are balanced and scored as hits versus false alarms to compute a sensitivity index (M-DPRIME) rather than raw caught-it counts.
learning_science.source: Green, D. M., & Swets, J. A. (1966). Signal Detection Theory and Psychophysics. Wiley.

learning_science.why: The accuracy of a child's confidence (calibration) adds incremental validity and lets scoring down-weight lucky guesses, sharpening tail decisions.
learning_science.concrete_decision: An optional post-verdict confidence tap on a subset yields a confidence-accuracy calibration signal (M-CONF) without adding burden to every trial.
learning_science.source: Nelson, T. O., & Narens, L. (1990). Metamemory: A theoretical framework and new findings. Psychology of Learning and Motivation, 26, 125-173.

learning_science.why: A spoken scene paired with a picture lets pre-readers make the plausibility judgment with no print, keeping the item near-language-neutral.
learning_science.concrete_decision: Young items are audio plus picture scenes with two large verdict doors; printed statements appear only from older bands with an audio option retained.
learning_science.source: Paivio, A. (1986). Mental Representations: A Dual Coding Approach. Oxford University Press.

tail_precision_rationale: Streaming many plausibility verdicts turns one unit into a graded score (M-POLY) and, because real and impossible scenes are balanced, into a signal-detection sensitivity (M-DPRIME) that separates true impossibility detection from a yes/impossible response bias exactly at the cut. Optional confidence taps (M-CONF) calibrate certainty and down-weight lucky guesses, M-ERRTYPE flags whether a miss was a subtle plausibility violation (latent ability just under threshold) versus a gross one, and the catch-the-only-impossible-among-plausible sets push the ceiling for gifted world-knowledge reasoning.
age_rationale: A two-door possible/impossible verdict on an audio-plus-picture scene with a single tap is valid at K-1; printed statements, subtler violations, the catch-the-only-impossible set, and confidence calibration extend it through 6-8. Reading load appears only in the older text mode and is offset by an audio option; the verdict doors are large fixed targets so motor demand stays low.

adaptive.content_range: Obvious physical or biological impossibilities among clearly-real everyday scenes (K-1) up to subtle plausibility violations and a single subtly-impossible scene hidden among several plausible ones (6-8).
adaptive.difficulty_levers: salience of the violation (gross physical impossibility -> subtle plausibility violation); base rate of impossible vs real scenes; picture-plus-audio vs printed text; statement length and syntactic complexity; presence of the confidence tap and the find-the-only-impossible set.
adaptive.notes: Scene templates with a swappable world-knowledge-violation slot and curated plausible foils; scenes tagged by violation type and plausibility; parallel forms swap same-band scenes at matched violation salience.

engagement_hook: Two doors - a sunny 'Real' door and a giggling 'Impossible' door; sending each scene through the right door fills a giggle-meter, and catching the sneaky impossible scene hiding among real ones is the big win.
construct_irrelevant_risks: World knowledge can be cultural (mitigated by universal physical and biological violations and dialect-neutral scenes); a yes-or-impossible response bias is controlled by balancing the real/impossible base rate and reporting sensitivity (M-DPRIME) rather than raw hits; reading load only in the older text mode (audio option; picture scenes for young); short scenes plus one replay cap listening and attention load; large fixed verdict doors keep motor noise low.

name: Umbrella Words
one_liner: See a few pictures (named aloud) and tap the one word that covers them all - not too narrow, not too broad.
interaction: 3-4 member pictures appear under an umbrella and are read aloud; the child taps one of four category-word buttons (each spoken on tap). The correct choice is the smallest word that still covers every member. A single tap commits, then the correct umbrella word lights green.
self_teach: A <10s wordless clip shows dog/cat/horse under the umbrella while a ghost hand taps 'Animals' (lights green) as 'Dog', 'Living things' and 'Leash' stay grey; one unscored warm-up (balls) runs before scoring. Pictures + audio mean no reading is needed.

learning_science.why: Abstracting a set to its category label indexes semantic-hierarchy reasoning, distinct from picking another member of the set.
learning_science.concrete_decision: Difficulty lever is the taxonomic level of the target word (basic 'fruit' up to abstract 'emotions'); the three distractors are a too-narrow member, a too-broad superset, and a thematic associate.
learning_science.source: Rosch, E. (1975). Cognitive representations of semantic categories. Journal of Experimental Psychology: General.

learning_science.why: The associate lure tests whether the child separates true category membership from mere thematic association, a semantic-control read.
learning_science.concrete_decision: Include exactly one thematic-associate distractor per item and tag which lure class an error picks.
learning_science.source: Collins, A. & Loftus, E. (1975). A spreading-activation theory of semantic processing. Psychological Review.

learning_science.why: A wordless demo removes instruction-language load so the mechanic self-teaches in <10s.
learning_science.concrete_decision: Ghost-hand demo plus one unscored warm-up before scoring begins.
learning_science.source: Sweller, J. (2006). The worked example effect and human cognition. Learning and Instruction.

tail_precision_rationale: Superordinate abstraction ceilings later than picking a coordinate member, so an adaptive taxonomic-level staircase (M-DIFFREACH) plus the lexical frequency of the solved category words (M-VOCABLVL) keeps separating gifted lexical/relational depth after basic categories saturate. The lure profile (M-LURETYPE: too-narrow vs too-broad vs associate) turns each error into graded evidence - a too-broad slip at high abstraction marks near-threshold ability, refining tail placement beyond right/wrong.
age_rationale: Single-tap choice with audio + pictures works for pre-readers (K-1) using basic categories; abstract, low-frequency category words extend the ceiling for 6-8. No reading or fine motor beyond a tap.

adaptive.content_range: basic concrete categories (animals, fruit) up to abstract superordinates (emotions, tools, travel gear) and low-frequency labels
adaptive.difficulty_levers: taxonomic level/abstractness of the target; lexical frequency of the correct word; taxonomic distance of the too-narrow/too-broad lures; strength of the thematic associate
adaptive.notes: Generator picks a category, samples N members, and auto-builds the four lure classes from a tagged noun hierarchy; frequency bands come from a Zipf-tagged lexicon.

engagement_hook: Raise the umbrella that shelters everybody - a quick, satisfying 'aha' as the right big word lights up.
construct_irrelevant_risks: Vocabulary exposure (mitigated by frequency-leveling and audio+picture support so category reasoning, not decoding, is tested); cultural familiarity of members (use universal basics at low bands); avoid regional labels; ensure the too-broad lure is a genuine superset, not a second valid answer.

name: Two Meanings
one_liner: Hear a word that has two meanings inside a spoken sentence, then tap the picture that shows the meaning the sentence points to.
interaction: A homograph is shown and a sentence using it is read aloud (and printed for readers). Four pictures appear: the sentence-appropriate meaning, the OTHER meaning of the same word, a thematic associate, and an unrelated foil. One tap selects; the correct meaning then lights green.
self_teach: Wordless demo: 'The BAT flew around the dark cave' plays while a ghost hand taps the flying-bat picture (green) and the baseball-bat picture stays grey; one unscored warm-up before scoring. Audio + pictures mean no reading is needed.

learning_science.why: Selecting a word's meaning from sentence context indexes semantic control and comprehension monitoring beyond raw vocabulary.
learning_science.concrete_decision: Difficulty lever is context-bias strength and whether the biased meaning is dominant or subordinate; the OTHER-meaning picture is always present as the key competitor.
learning_science.source: Swinney, D. (1979). Lexical access during sentence comprehension. Journal of Verbal Learning and Verbal Behavior.

learning_science.why: Forcing the subordinate meaning taxes controlled retrieval, the tail-relevant skill.
learning_science.concrete_decision: Later levels bias the less-frequent meaning so strong comprehenders who suppress the dominant reading are separated.
learning_science.source: Rodd, J., Gaskell, G. & Marslen-Wilson, W. (2002). Making sense of semantic ambiguity. Journal of Memory and Language.

learning_science.why: Spoken sentence + pictures removes decoding load so the task self-teaches.
learning_science.concrete_decision: Ghost-hand demo + one unscored trial; audio is replayable.
learning_science.source: Mayer, R. (2005). Cambridge Handbook of Multimedia Learning (modality principle).

tail_precision_rationale: Mapping bias strength to inference depth (M-INFDEPTH: strong-literal up to subtle-subordinate) records the deepest disambiguation a child sustains, which keeps separating strong comprehenders after literal items ceiling. Because the OTHER-meaning picture is always present, choosing it (vs an associate or unrelated foil) is a diagnostic near-miss (M-LURETYPE/M-ERRTYPE) that localizes latent ability just below the cut; an adaptive frequency staircase (M-VOCABLVL/M-DIFFREACH) individualizes the frontier.
age_rationale: Spoken sentence + picture choice is accessible to pre-readers (K-1) with high-frequency homographs and strong context; subtle context and subordinate, low-frequency meanings extend the ceiling to 6-8.

adaptive.content_range: concrete high-frequency homographs (bat, bark, ring) with strong context up to low-frequency words with subtle/subordinate-meaning context
adaptive.difficulty_levers: context-bias strength; dominant vs subordinate target meaning; word frequency; similarity of the associate lure
adaptive.notes: Clone by pairing a homograph with a meaning-biasing sentence frame and four tagged pictures; needs a curated homograph+picture bank (picture availability limits full auto-generation).

engagement_hook: One word, two secret meanings - be the detective who catches which one the sentence really means.
construct_irrelevant_risks: Picture recognizability (use clear, culturally neutral images); listening load (short, replayable sentences); vocabulary exposure (frequency-level words, support with audio); ensure exactly one picture fits the sentence so the key is unambiguous.

name: Clue Chain
topics_techniques_covered: linear-syllogism / transitive inference: chain 2-4 spoken comparative premises (a Wug is taller than a Blip; a Blip is taller than a Zorf) to a superlative or ordering stated in no single clue
categorical & conditional deduction: integrate all/some or if-then premises to reach an unstated conclusion
one_liner: Hear a few clues that link creatures (bigger, faster, older), then work out the answer no single clue tells you - like who is biggest - by chaining the clues together.
interaction: Two to four spoken (and shown) comparison clues appear as cards using made-up creature names (a Wug is taller than a Blip; a Blip is taller than a Zorf). The clues stay visible so the task is reasoning, not memory. The child taps the creature that answers a question whose answer is stated in no single clue (who is TALLEST?), or, in the ordering variant, drags the creatures into order. One tap (or one ordering) submits; audio replays on demand; no reading required.
self_teach: Wordless demo: three creatures, two clues read aloud (Wug>Blip, Blip>Zorf); a ghost hand taps Wug for 'tallest' and it lights green, showing the winner appears in no single clue; then one unscored warm-up. Made-up names + audio + pictures mean no vocabulary or reading is needed.

learning_science.why: Deriving an unstated relation from linked premises indexes relational reasoning and construction of an integrated mental model, a core reasoning skill vocabulary-heavy verbal items miss.
learning_science.concrete_decision: Premises are adjacent links in a hidden order presented in scrambled sequence so the child must integrate rather than read off; difficulty rises by chain length (2->4 premises); premises stay visible to keep it reasoning, not span.
learning_science.source: Halford, G. et al. (1998). Processing capacity defined by relational complexity. Behavioral and Brain Sciences.

learning_science.why: Nonsense creature names and abstract relations strip out vocabulary/cultural knowledge so the score reflects reasoning, not word exposure - the area's bias-mitigation discipline.
learning_science.concrete_decision: All entities are invented (Wug, Blip, Zorf); relations are perceptual comparatives; content is delivered by audio plus pictures.
learning_science.source: Sternberg, R. (1980). Representation and process in linear syllogistic reasoning. Journal of Experimental Psychology: General.

learning_science.why: Spoken plus pictured premises remove decoding load so the task self-teaches in under 10s.
learning_science.concrete_decision: Ghost-hand demo plus one unscored warm-up; clues remain on screen and audio is replayable.
learning_science.source: Mayer, R. (2005). Cambridge Handbook of Multimedia Learning (modality principle).

tail_precision_rationale: Chain length is a relational-complexity ladder: M-RULEID/M-ORALSPAN record the most premises a child binds into one model on correct items, separating children who all pass 2-premise items by pushing to 3-4 co-acting links; M-DIFFREACH escalates chain length to failure to pinpoint the edge. Because distractors are the other creatures in the order, choosing the NEXT-in-order creature is a diagnostic near-miss (M-ERRTYPE) that localizes latent ability just below the cut, while random-position errors mark non-integration. Parallel matched chains (M-CONSIST) tighten the standard error near the cut; the ordering variant adds partial credit (M-POLY). Keeping premises visible makes this a reasoning, not a memory-span, signal.
age_rationale: A 2-premise concrete comparison with pictures and audio is within reach at K-1 (transitive inference emerges by ~4-5 years with visible premises and scaffolding); the ceiling extends by adding premises (3-4 links), scrambling premise order, and introducing categorical (all/some), conditional (if-then), and negated clues for grades 4-5 and 6-8. Premises stay visible so working-memory load does not gate the youngest band.

adaptive.content_range: 2-premise concrete comparatives (taller/faster) up to 4-premise scrambled chains and mixed categorical/conditional/negated deductions
adaptive.difficulty_levers: number of premises (chain length); congruent vs scrambled premise order; superlative vs middle-term question; comparative vs categorical/conditional relation; presence of a negation; similarity of the near-miss (adjacent) foil
adaptive.notes: Fully procedurally generated: sample k creatures, a random hidden order, adjacent-link premises in scrambled display, and one keyed question; distractors are the other creatures so each foil maps to a rank distance.

engagement_hook: Be the detective who cracks the case with clues that never spell out the answer - you have to link them yourself.
construct_irrelevant_risks: Working-memory load (kept low by leaving all premises visible as anchor cards, so the task measures integration not storage); listening load (short, replayable spoken clues plus printed text for readers); picture/name discriminability (distinct colours and simple invented names); ensure exactly one creature follows logically so the key is unambiguous; avoid real-word names that could import prior knowledge.
